posts.title: Area51 and Area West sound like one place, and the sources say they are two
posts.subtitle: A skatepark in a former Philips hall on Strijp-S and a Dutch Design Week area south of it, followed through planning and press records, the organizers' own pages and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Area51 and Area West: two names, two places
posts.description: A Strijp-S skatepark and a DDW area south of it: what planning, press and program records say about each, from 2006 to DDW 2026.

r: Area51 and Area West sound like one place in Eindhoven, and every source I opened treats them as two.

In anatomy I learned to check whether two names point at one structure before I assume they do, because a shared name is where wrong assumptions start. This essay uses public sources only: a tourist board, a district site, contractor and developer pages, trade and local press, Dutch Design Week's own pages and its photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about what is on show during DDW 2026 beyond what the published listings say.

blocks.x: Area51 is a hall on Strijp-S with a skatepark at its center

r: Area51 is an indoor skatepark at Ketelhuisplein 18 on Strijp-S.
The tourist board calls it "the largest indoor skate park in the Benelux," and I treat that as the venue's and the tourist board's own claim, since no source I opened ranks it against other parks.

The venue's site describes a street section with ledges and rails, a park section with a six-meter vertical wall, a small bowl, a foam pit, a café overlooking the course, an event space and a basement venue.
The tourist board adds four dance studios and the Academy 51 lessons.

So the building holds more than skating, and that matters for the archive question later. A label that names a skatepark gets attached to dance, design fairs and a conference lounge, and the label keeps working because the address does.

blocks.x: The hall is a Philips building, and it has a code: SEU

r: The district site for Strijp-S calls the building SEU and says it is split in two. Area51 occupies one part and several other parties use the other, among them 040 BMX Park. The same page describes SEU as a former Philips machine factory, tall enough inside for BMX riding.
The tourist board's A to Z gives a different description: the building was a former tool shop and was among the first on the site to be repurposed after Philips left.

A machine factory and a tool shop can be the same place described two ways, and I do not claim to settle it. Neither page gives a construction year or says which Philips unit worked there. I found no heritage record for the building. A 2015 report quotes Trudo's director calling it architecturally unremarkable but charming, which is an opinion and not a register entry.
The same 2015 report places the hall between the residential building Anton and the Klokgebouw.

Strijp-S as a whole gives the frame. The district's history page says VolkerWessels and the municipality of Eindhoven bought the fenced Philips site in 2002 and leased it back to Philips, who stayed as the main user for several years. It says the fence was moved back gradually as Philips parts relocated, so that the first buildings became available for new use, and it ties Dutch Design Week choosing Strijp-S as its new home to the same period without giving a year.
The tourist board repeats the local nickname for the closed site, the forbidden city.

blocks.x: Skating here since 2006, and an older story about Meerhoven

r: Three sources date the use of the hall as a skatepark to 2006. A roofing contractor's project page says the hall has been in use since the fall of 2006.
A news item from the district site, dated January 16, 2023, says Area51 has been at Ketelhuisplein since 2006.
A skate magazine's park review of September 2014 says the same, and it adds an older story: the park opened in 2000 in an old aircraft hangar in Meerhoven, which is where the name Area51 comes from.

Another source disagrees on the founding. A design furniture retailer's blog, writing in November 2011 after a visit during Dutch Design Week, says Area 51 was established in 2002, in an old industrial building on the former Philips estate.

The 2002 and 2000 dates cannot both be right for the first park, and only the magazine mentions Meerhoven. I settle one thing and leave one open. The move to Strijp-S in 2006 has three sources that do not obviously copy each other, a contractor, a district site and a skate magazine. The year the first park opened, and where, has one source for 2000 and one for 2002, and I treat both as second-hand.

The blog gives a useful picture of the hall in 2011 all the same. It says the writers make time at every Dutch Design Week to leave the design fair and visit the skatepark, describes about 3,000 square meters of landscaped wood, and says Area 51 shows that city planning needs space for teenagers too.
That makes the hall a stop for design visitors years before the photo archive in this series begins. It is a blog's account, and it does not say anything was exhibited there.

blocks.x: The hall nearly went, and then homes were built over it

r: In 2015 the hall's future was open. Innovation Origins reported on October 10, 2015 that the urban plan for the site called for the old factory hall, between Anton and the Klokgebouw, to make way for housing. It says the hall was supposed to be gone already, to give way to a residential tower with a technology and media museum called Volt at its base, and that one of the museum's initiators, the Hilversum museum Beeld en Geluid, withdrew at the end of 2013, which put the tower and the demolition on hold.

Jack Hock, the Trudo director responsible for developing Strijp-S, then proposed keeping the hall and building homes across it: three levels of apartments on a structure that would span the skatepark and the BMX hall like a bridge. The report quotes him saying the site had lost too much to demolition already, and it quotes the Area51 manager as pleased and cautious, since the municipality and VolkerWessels would decide.

That plan became Haasje Over. Trudo's page says the Amsterdam architect VMX designed it, with a tower of 19 floors, about 70 meters high, and a bridge building of two residential layers across the existing skatehal, with homes of social rent.
The builder Stam + De Koning describes the bridge as an air bridge of about 50 homes, six meters high, running over the skatehal, and speaks of the building in the past tense, as finished.

The consultancy Tielemans's project page describes two bridges of 50 meters each, built as trusses and carrying dwellings above the existing hall, and a footbridge from Haasje Over to the roof of Anton on the tenth floor.
Trudo's page expected the first homes to be delivered in January and February 2021.
The sources differ on the tower's lofts: Trudo's pre-completion page counts 136, the builder's page counts 134.

Neither figure matters to Area51, so I name both and leave it. What the sources do not say is how building above the hall changed daily life inside it. The district's history page only says the hall is no longer to be demolished and is fitted into the new plans.

blocks.x: Two parks became one in a rebuild around 2020 and 2021

r: The next change came from the inside. On November 9, 2018 Innovation Origins reported that an upgrade of Area 51 was among the first ten projects to receive money from the Regio Deal Brainport Eindhoven, a program in which the national government would invest 130 million euros and the region 240 million over four years in the area's business climate.

A quote in the report says the upgrade would create a location with wide pull in the region and abroad, where both recreational and top athletes could train. The amount awarded to Area51 is not in the text I read, and I leave it out.

A Brainport Eindhoven profile of a regular tells the rest in a teenager's words. It says renovation work ran in 2020 and 2021, that the venue used to have one area for skaters and another for scooter riders and BMX riders, and that the course is now much bigger. It reports that people now come by train from other cities, and that more visitors come from abroad.
The profile is undated in the text I read, and it is a feature written to show what the program paid for.

The venue's own pages describe the result today. The course is given as 3,000 square meters, with the street section's 750 square meters serving as an event floor, a cellar of 355 square meters with its own entrance on Ketelhuisplein, a café with room for 350 people and a multi-purpose room of 190 square meters.
The tourist board's location page says 2,800 square meters.
I use "about 3,000 square meters" for the course because the venue's page gives that figure, and I name the venue as the source.

blocks.x: Before the archive: a blog visit in 2011 and the opening night of 2023

r: Dutch Design Week came into the hall twice in ways the photo archive does not show. The first is the 2011 visit above. The second is the Grand Opening of DDW23. A DDW news item dated October 21, 2023 says the week began with a Grand Opening in the heart of the skatepark at Area 51, hosted by Lynn Zebeda and Cesar Majorana, with a takeover by The New Originals and guests named as Phantom Wizard, Fumez, Sokarekta and TNO Sound. It says the creative head of DDW opened with the theme Picture This.
Area51's own event-location page lists the opening of Dutch Design Week among the non-urban-sports events it has hosted, next to Club Vrijdag and the Storioni Festival.
The two pages agree. The news item's date is the date of the page, and it does not say which evening the opening was. I did not find the evening elsewhere.
In the archive albums I read on October 7, 2026, the 2023 Area51 album holds five photos, all of an artists' collaboration. It has no photo of the opening night.
A single exhibition stands for the venue in 2023, and the biggest night of the week there is not in the album. I did not check every album in the account, so I limit the point to the albums I read.

blocks.x: 2023: a drawing machine and four hands

r: The 2023 album's photos are titled Antigoon 2023, and they credit Almicheal Fraay.

A listing in DDW's own program explains the project. The listing says that before and during DDW 2023 Antigoon and the graphic design duo Thomas & Jurgen would make new work, to see what happens when a human and machine collaboration meets a human and human one, and that the results would be presented at Area 51.

It describes Antigoon as building machines that combine a program's binary logic with intentional anomalies from the human programmer, and Thomas & Jurgen as working with self-made tools to move ink or paint across glass, perspex or brick.
St. Joost School of Art & Design separately lists its tutor's display as Antigoon X Thomas & Jurgen at Area 51.

All three artists are part of UC MASTERS, which the listing says gives talented artists a grant and guidance. It is a project by EMOVES, supported by Cultuur Eindhoven, the province of North Brabant and the national education and culture ministry.
The tourist board says Area51, the youth center Dynamo and The Ruggeds form EMOVES together, which places the venue inside the organization behind the program, as I read it.
The photos show a bright white-brick hall with tall windows, a flat-bed drawing machine on a black table, a person drawing on a window, framed prints on the floor and a black display wall.
The listing's description fits what the photos show. I cannot say which machine in a photo belongs to Antigoon, and I describe the objects by how they look.

blocks.x: 2024: a design fair takes the building, and the archive tags another place

r: In 2024 Isola Design, a design platform that also stages a Milan showcase, took over Area51. Its press text, as Archisearch reported it on October 22, 2024, says this was its sixth consecutive participation in Dutch Design Week, which ran from October 19 to 27, 2024, with more than 100 exhibitors in four exhibitions that would share the building with the skaters' regular activities.
DDW's program listing says the same four exhibitions were inspired by the theme This Future is Currently Unavailable.

The sources place the exhibitions floor by floor. Disclosure took the basement, with more than 40 independent designers and studios. Forms Unfolding and Routes to Roots took the ground floor, where the second was a traveling show made with a cultural center in Saudi Arabia and seen earlier in Saudi Arabia and in Milan. The Floor is Yours took the first floor, in a dance studio. The café on the first floor served as the meeting and talk area.
The sources disagree on one number. Archisearch gives the basement space as 350 square meters and DDW's listing as 300.
The venue's own page gives the cellar as 355.
I take "about 350" because two of the three agree and the venue's measurement sits beside it, and I name that as a reading, since I found no measurement.

The photo archive has no Area51 album for 2024. It has two albums tagged AreaWest in their photo titles, Fashion Tech Farm with 11 photos and Next Nature Museum at the Evoluon with seven, both by Tommy Köhlbrugge.
A reader scanning the archive for Area51 in 2024 would find nothing and might conclude the venue was unused. The press says it was full.

blocks.x: Area West is a label on DDW's own map

r: DDW's own pages explain the second name. The 2024 area recap says the West area lies just south of Strijp-S and is home to the Evoluon, which it calls the Next Nature Museum.
The 2026 locations list gives West as a filter of its own, next to Canal, Center, Hallenweg, Sectie-C, Station, Strijp-S and Strijp T+R.
The Fashion Tech Farm's 2026 listing gives its address as Zeelsterstraat 80 in the West area.
DDW's page for Area 51 lists the area as Strijp-S.

So the archive labels follow DDW's labels, and the confusion belongs to a reader. The tag AreaWest in a 2024 photo title is accurate for the farm and the Evoluon. The label "Area51" in 2023 and 2025 is accurate for the skatepark. I found no source that ties the two names together. In the record they share a sound and nothing else.

blocks.x: 2025: four exhibitions, one album of 73 photos and a lounge

r: DDW's program pages for 2025 place four projects at Area 51. Next, Now, Then by the German Design Council presents German graduation projects. Hochschule Trier's news item says it showed 25 projects from October 18 to 26, 2025, curated by the studio Raw Colour.
Red Box, a program on design that strengthens the position of women, names Stoov as its main sponsor and lists 15 participants, with talks and workshops at several locations in the city.
Seeds of Hope shows the work of 15 Fontys graduates in Trend Research and Concept Creation in Lifestyle, five new exhibitors every three days.

Shaping the future of care, from the elder-care organization Anna Ouderenzorg and a dementia and technology center at the university in Eindhoven, listed a workshop at Area51 on Monday, October 20 from 10:00 to 12:00.

The archive holds two Area51 albums for the year. The first is nine photos of the German show by Max Kneefel. The second is a Business Lounge album with 73 photos by Kneefel and Cleo Goossens in the 24 titles I read.
The other three exhibitions have no Area51 album in the list I read. The year's archive coverage of the venue is one exhibition and one lounge.
The lounge now has an answer, with a limit. DDW's 2026 frequently asked questions say the Design Tours start at the DDW Business Lounge in Area51 on Ketelhuisplein.
One of the 2025 lounge photos carries a Design Tour title dated October 24, 2025, which fits.

I read this as the lounge being a base for tours in both years, and the 2025 half is my inference from one photo title. The sponsors on the lounge sign are visible in the photographs, and I did not find a page saying who they were.
The four 2025 program pages I opened name other organizers, and I found no page placing Isola Design at Area51 in 2025. That does not prove it was absent, and the question stays open.

blocks.x: The archive leans on one year

r: The Area51 albums hold 87 photos and the two AreaWest albums 18, which makes 105. The 2025 albums hold 82 of them, 78 percent, and the Business Lounge album alone holds 73. The 2024 albums hold 18 and 2023 holds five.
Anyone counting photos per year would conclude 2025 mattered most. The counts show what was photographed and uploaded, and I would not read more into them than that.

blocks.x: 2026: four items on DDW's list

r: DDW's 2026 page for the location lists nine days of opening hours, October 17 to 25, from 11:00 to 18:00, and free access.

It lists four items. Fontys for Society, run all week, is a Fontys exhibition in five zones named Think, Create, Tech, Apply and Reflect, according to a FRITS news item that also says visitors need no DDW ticket.

SpaceTeen, also all week, is a research and design project in which young people work with designers and scientists on alternatives to social media, from a University of Amsterdam research group, a design studio, a digital design agency and a social design agency.

Philips Design. Soul & Science runs across the Philips Museum, Area51 and the streets, and its description puts the part at Area51 under the heading care felt. The credits on the listing include a board member of Area51 as an exhibition host.

The fourth is Open Socials Social Club on Friday, October 23, by Waag Futurelab, a party that marks the soft launch of an open social media platform and puts on stage artists the listing says Meta had banned.
A party in a skatepark belongs to a hall with a basement venue and an event floor.

The venue's own Dutch Design Week page needs a careful reading. When I opened it on October 9, 2026, it still said that Dutch Design Week 2025 was getting closer, and the home page teasers for the festival carried placeholder text.
I read both as leftover text, and I rely on DDW's listing for 2026.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: 2006, from three sources. A 2011 blog says Area 51 was established in 2002 and a 2014 magazine says the park opened in 2000 in Meerhoven. I use 2006 for Strijp-S and leave the first park's year open.
A machine factory in one source and a tool shop in another. Not settled, and the phrase "former tool shop" is the tourist board's.
2,800 square meters on the tourist board's page, 3,000 on the venue's. I use the venue's figure for the course and name it.
300, 350 and 355 square meters. I use about 350 and name the venue's cellar figure.
136 on Trudo's page, 134 on the builder's.
DDW's own labels settle it. Area51 is in the Strijp-S area, and West is a separate area south of Strijp-S.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know the year the SEU hall was built, which Philips unit used it, or whether it is a registered monument. I found no heritage record for it.
I do not know when the first Area51 opened, or whether it began in Meerhoven in 2000 or elsewhere in 2002.
I do not know what building Haasje Over above the hall changed for the skatepark's daily use.
I do not know the amount the Regio Deal gave Area51, and I could not open the news item that reportedly states it.
I do not know the date of the Brainport profile.
I do not know which evening the DDW23 opening took place, or whether other albums in the archive hold photos of it.
I do not know why the archive has no Area51 album for 2024, whether Isola Design returned in 2025, or who the sponsors on the lounge sign were.
I read only 24 of the Business Lounge album's 73 titles, and I did not reopen the photo archive for this version.

If you look up a venue in an archive, try three questions. Is the label a building or an area? Does the album title match the place in the photo? And does the archive skip a year the venue was in use? Area51 gives a clear answer to the last one, because 2024 is missing from its albums and full in the press.

posts.title: Design Perron sounds like a station platform, and its address is a building on Fuutlaan
posts.subtitle: A former freight-forwarding building a five-minute walk from Eindhoven's central station, the venue's own history, and nine editions in the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Design Perron: a building on Fuutlaan, not a platform
posts.description: Design Perron in Eindhoven from 2013 to a final edition at Fuutlaan 12 in 2026: the building, the DDW record and what the sources leave open.

r: The name Design Perron points to a railway platform, and the sources I opened point to a building on Fuutlaan that was once used to move freight.

DDW's 2026 page for the location says Design Perron is held in the building of Opvallers at Fuutlaan 12 and calls it a five-minute walk from the central station. It lists opening hours of 11:00 to 18:00 from October 17 to 24, 2026 and 11:00 to 17:00 on October 25, with free access.
Design Perron's own 2026 notice adds something the older records could not: the area is being redeveloped, the building's tenant has to move, and this will be the last edition at Fuutlaan 12.

This essay uses public sources only: Design Perron's pages, DDW's program pages and archive, a regional archive record, a property listing, press from 2013 and 2014 and the municipality's project page. It reports no visit and no interview.

blocks.x: The name points to the station, and DDW files the place under "Station"

r: Perron is the Dutch word for a station platform. Design Perron's English page uses the line "a track full of design stories," and its 2026 notice calls the building a station of ideas, materials, encounters and new designs for nine days.

The national monuments register lists Eindhoven's station, built in 1956 to a design by K. van der Gaast and registered on March 29, 2010, and its protected parts include the platforms, perrons in Dutch.
DDW adds to the confusion without meaning to. Its 2026 locations list sorts places by area, and Design Perron sits in the area called Station.
DDW's 2024 recap of the Station area walks through projects around the station building.

Earlier years used other words. A DDW magazine recap of 2018 called the area from the station to the NRE site Central, and the 2019 area text said the central station marks the heart of a new design area and sent visitors to Design Perron alongside the railroad track.

As an anatomist I learned that a structure's name and its location are two separate facts, and that a good atlas gives both. A venue name needs the same treatment. Read the name for what it suggests and the address for where the place is.

blocks.x: The building: freight shed, theater premises, office

r: Fuutlaan 12 has a longer record than the festival. The regional historical center for Eindhoven holds a photograph titled Fuutlaan 12, forwarding company Van Gend & Loos, 1973.

A commercial property listing for one unit, Fuutlaan 12 E1, says the complex lies directly against the railway beside the central station, was formerly used by Van Gend & Loos to move goods from trucks to rail wagons, and dates from 1956 according to the national address register.
The same listing names Opvallers among the creative businesses around it.

A fire brigade report on a fire of October 8, 1955 describes a 150-meter freight shed of the railways, with the Van Gend & Loos loading station, burning in the direction of the station building, and it says the new shed would be in use within months.
The report does not give a street, so I cannot tie the fire to Fuutlaan 12. The dates are consistent with a replacement shed in 1956, and I leave it at that.
Design Perron's own history adds the next layer. Its team page says the building Opvallers showed founder Meike van Schijndel in 2013 was the old premises of the theater company Het Zuidelijk Toneel.
A Utrecht news site, writing on December 11, 2013 about that October, says she showed the Delta vase in the old Zuidelijk Toneel building.

That is independent support from 2013 for the building's earlier use, though it is one line in a profile and I have found no record of the theater company's years there. Opvallers describes itself on its own site as a company that runs face-to-face campaigns and events, with nearly 25 years of work and a team of 350.

blocks.x: 2013: twelve exhibitions, a vase and a boulevard

r: Design Perron says it was founded in 2013. Van Schijndel was looking for a location for an exhibition during Dutch Design Week to honor the relaunch of the Delta vase of 1981, designed by her father, the architect Mart van Schijndel, who lived from 1943 to 1999. After a long search she met Martin Damen of Opvallers on Fuutlaan, and the first year brought twelve exhibitions in and around the building, according to Design Perron.
The Utrecht news item confirms the vase, the 1981 date and the Eindhoven showing in October 2013, and adds that the glass vase is assembled from three plates bonded with silicone rather than blown.

Press at the time counted differently. Core77's highlights from October 31, 2013 describe three long warehouses next to the central station that were partly emptied to make room for Design Perron, a set of ten exhibits, and a separate exhibit by the collective Dutch Invertuals.
Twelve and ten are not the same count, and neither source says how it counted. I take both as honest and different.

Design Perron's own page says the first year was held in and around the Opvallers building. Core77 places Design Perron in warehouses next to the station. Together they make it very likely that the 2013 warehouses and the Opvallers building are one site, and I say "very likely" because no single page states it in both vocabularies.

The 2014 edition was the second. A shop's news item gives the dates as October 18 to 26, 2014 at Fuutlaan 12 to 14, calls Design Perron a boulevard of bold design talent, and says about ten exhibitions stood outside in containers, with Dutch Invertuals and JSPR as resident exhibitors and a drinks evening on Wednesday, October 22.

In 2016 Design Perron's own page says it was taking place for the fourth time at Fuutlaan 12 to 14, with new halls, a lecture room of about 238 square meters, a pop-up shop and a Design Meets Brands program planned with Opvallers. It also says a group called Working Friends would occupy the back of the building that fall and that the café would again serve coffee, tea and organic rolls.

blocks.x: Foundation, team and the scale it claims

r: The team page says Van Schijndel started Design Perron in 2013 as an ad hoc DDW location. An interior designer joined in 2014 and an architect in 2015, which made the first real team, and since June 2016 it has been a foundation.
Both of those early team members have since left, and Chris Ruhe took on a larger role from 2025.
The page says the event now has more than 50 exhibitors and over 16,000 visitors a year. Those are the organizer's own figures, and I found no independent count.

For 2025, the info page gives Fuutlaan 12, 12A and 12E, with the designer market in 12 and 12A, a light lab at 12A and the graduates at 12E, October 18 to 26, 2025, open only during DDW, and free. It puts the walk at about five minutes from the central station, past the Effenaar.
A DDW notice dated September 30, 2025 about new exhibition clusters called HUBS names a Young Graduates HUB at Fuutlaan 12.

blocks.x: Who shows there: schools, collectives and brands

r: The exhibitor mix has stayed close to what the 2013 format promised. The 2014 notice lists Dutch Invertuals and JSPR as residents and names Cor Unum Ceramics, a second-year Design Academy Eindhoven master's group, a Utrecht platform for beginning talent and a Rotterdam group of creatives among many others.
Design Perron's 2016 page says a hall fitted out by Sint Lucas the year before could be rented for lectures and events.

In 2023 seven design graduates of the Berlin University of the Arts showed under the title U don't Know at Fuutlaan 12, open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 with free admission during DDW23, October 21 to 29, 2023, according to the university's own page.

The former-exhibitors page is a long run of image galleries by year, and the labels on its images name schools such as ArtEZ, Artemis Academy, Cibap, HKU, the Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences and the Willem de Kooning Academy, next to studios, ceramicists and brands.

I read those as labels set by Design Perron, and I did not count exhibitors. The 2026 mix repeats the pattern: a Swedish textile school, a brand and designer pairing, a designer market and a disability arts organization.

blocks.x: What the archive and the venue's own site show for each year

r: The official DDW Flickr archive holds albums named Design Perron for nine editions: 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2025, with 157 photos in total.

The photographers are credited in the titles. In 2015 the 15 photos credit Cleo Goossens and Boudewijn Bollmann and name Hamerhaai and Studio Ineke van der Werff, and one shows a sign reading opvallers. The venue's own pictures page for 2015 carries labels such as Cor Unum, Ineke van der Werff, Ultra Studio, MVOS and Hamerhaai, which match some of the photo titles.
The 2016 album has 26 photos by Tommy Köhlbrugge. The 2017 album has 11 by Bollmann, including a painted sign reading "Een spoor vol design," Dutch for a track full of design.

Britt Roelse shot the eight photos of 2018, Nick Bookelaar the eight of 2019, whose titles name the designer Marlou Beentjes, and Roelse again the 24 of 2021 and 22 of 2022, both titled FUUTLAAN_DESIGNPERRON. Almicheal Fraay shot the 19 of 2023, and Goossens the 24 of 2025, all titled DesignPerron_Station_DDW25.
The DDW 2018 magazine says the venue again offered a stage to many designers.
In 2023 DDW listed a drinks evening for ten years of Design Perron from 17:00 to 20:00 at Fuutlaan 12.
The 2025 file titles have a likely explanation. Station is DDW's area label for the venue, and the titles begin DesignPerron_Station.
The titles do not say why the photographers chose the word, so that reading is mine.

blocks.x: Two missing years that were not missing

r: The archive has no album named Design Perron for 2020 or 2024, and I first read that as a gap in the event. The venue's own site says otherwise. Its info page for 2020 sets out the pandemic rules: every DDW location needed a DDW ticket that year, checked at the door, and Design Perron could only be entered with one.
Its former-exhibitors page carries a gallery for every year from 2013 to 2025, 2020 and 2024 included.
So the event ran in 2020 by its own page, and the 2024 gallery label points the same way. The archive does not file photographs of those years under its name.

For 2024 the archive has two small albums with related titles, Fuutlaan with five photos and Centraal Station Eindhoven with two, neither named Design Perron. A 2023 album titled Fuutlaan 12C holds 14 photos by Fraay, and a 2025 album titled Centraal Station Eindhoven holds 27 by Max Kneefel. The archive does not link any of these to Design Perron.
An album named for the station tells you where a photographer stood and not which venue the pictures show.

blocks.x: 2026: the last edition at Fuutlaan 12

r: DDW's page for 2026 lists 11 entries at the location, among them the Swedish School of Textiles show EXIT26, a furniture and textile exhibition, a workshop that appears twice, a mahjong project, a shelving system and a vase exhibition by Special Arts in which creators with disabilities answer the question what a vase is.

Brands & Designers pairs brands and designers and was originally developed for a three-day festival in Amsterdam. It was designed by Van Schijndel, and four of its original eight houses are shown here.

Design Perron's drinks notice invites visitors on Monday, October 19 from 17:00 to 20:00 to celebrate 13 years and 13 editions on Fuutlaan 12 and thanks Damen and the Opvallers team for their hospitality.

By the site's own year galleries, 2013 to 2025 is 13 editions, which would make 2026 the fourteenth. Either "13 editions" counts through 2025 or it counts elapsed years, and the page does not say which.
The two sources also disagree on where the graduates will be. Design Perron's 2026 home page places a Young Graduates Hub with 30 graduates at Kennedyplein 300, a second location.

DDW's 2026 locations list shows Design Perron at Fuutlaan 12 and I found no Kennedyplein 300 entry on it, and DDW's own notice names the Young Graduates HUB at Fuutlaan 12, though that notice dates from September 30, 2025.
I do not know which is current. DDW's 2026 page for the venue also says other exhibits there come from Dutch Invertuals, Envisions, Spoor K, JSPR and others.

blocks.x: The area is being redeveloped

r: Design Perron says the area is being redeveloped and Opvallers has to move.

The municipality's project page for the Nieuwe Fuutlaan says the city council adopted a Fuutlaan area framework in 2024, that the first step is a new road between Stationsweg and the Insulindelaan ring, and that the city, NS and ProRail carry it out. It gives a schedule: research in 2026, a design phase and permit procedure in 2027, and execution from 2028 to 2030.
The page does not name Opvallers, the building or Design Perron, so the link between the two statements is Design Perron's own. I did not find a document naming the building.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: DDW's address and the property record settle it. The venue is a building on Fuutlaan, and the station appears as a walking reference.
Design Perron's own count for 2013 is twelve, Core77's is ten. Not settled.
They did, by the venue's own pages. The archive lacks albums under the name.
Where the graduates will be in 2026.
Fuutlaan 12 on DDW's list, Kennedyplein 300 on Design Perron's page. Not settled.
Counted from the galleries, 13 ends in 2025. Not settled.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know who owned the Fuutlaan 12 complex over the years, or whether the Opvallers building is the replacement shed that the 1955 report anticipates. I did not find a heritage record, and that report does not give an address.
I do not know how long Het Zuidelijk Toneel used the building, or in what way. The company is named in Design Perron's account and in one news profile, and I found no record from the theater side.

I do not know why the archive files no photographs under Design Perron for 2020 and 2024, whether the 2024 Fuutlaan photographs show the venue, or who the exhibitors are in photographs whose titles carry no name. I read the album pages on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen the archive for this version, so counts and credits come from that reading.
I do not know where the venue will go after 2026, or whether the Young Graduates Hub is at Fuutlaan 12 or Kennedyplein 300.

If you plan to visit during DDW 2026, check the address on DDW's location page before you set out. When you open a venue's photo archive, which would you trust first: the name, the file title, or the address on this year's listing?

posts.title: A building made to show the future has to keep updating it
posts.subtitle: The Evoluon in Eindhoven, from Philips's 1961 decision to its 2018 sale and the Next Nature Museum, read through the records and four Dutch Design Week archive years
posts.seoTitle: The Evoluon: a building made to show the future
posts.description: The Evoluon from the 1961 Philips decision to the Next Nature Museum and four DDW photo albums, with what the records do and do not show.

r: A museum built to show the future has to keep revising the future it shows, and the Evoluon in Eindhoven was designed on that principle in 1961.
The Philips Museum's own account says the exhibition inside the Evoluon was meant to look ahead, to avoid being a showroom for Philips products, and to avoid lingering in the past.

That plan makes the later history easier to read. The Evoluon closed as a museum in 1989, spent years as a congress center, was sold by Philips for a new use and reopened in 2022 as the Next Nature Museum.

This essay follows the building through public records: Philips's museum, heritage and planning news, trade and regional press, Next Nature's own pages and annual report, and the official Dutch Design Week program and photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview.

In medical education I have seen what happens to a teaching collection that never updates, because it ends up teaching a past generation's anatomy. A science museum has the same problem on a larger scale, and the Evoluon is a good place to watch it.

blocks.x: Planned in 1961, opened on September 24, 1966

r: The Philips Museum records that on January 2, 1961 the board agreed to a proposal by Frits Philips: instead of taking part in world exhibitions, Philips would build a house for a museum and an ever-renewing exhibition of its products. The board's reasons included a spectacular marker for the company's 75th anniversary and a place to receive the many visitors who could not be taken through the factories. After the Brussels world exhibition of 1958, where Philips made a good impression with its own pavilion, the board had decided against joining further fairs.

Philips had shown products in Eindhoven before. The museum lists a prewar history museum in the company school, destroyed in a bombing raid on December 6, 1942, a Demonstration Laboratory of 1951, which is today's Philips Museum, and a product studio of 1948.

The museum also names a possible inspiration, the Dome of Discovery at the Festival of Britain in 1951, for which Kalff gave lighting advice, and it notes that he also advised on the lighting of the festival's pleasure gardens in Battersea Park, designed by James Gardner, who later shaped the Evoluon exhibition.

Louis Kalff, who the museum says headed Philips Design from 1925 to 1960, made the first sketches. According to Frits Philips's autobiography as the museum quotes it, the building that looked like a spaceship was drawn over lunch on the back of a menu.
A heritage site tells the story differently: a dinner at which Kalff drew three designs, one of them the flying saucer, and it adds that this is tradition.
Omroep Brabant has a lunch with a menu.

I take the menu as the story's fixed point and leave the meal open. The museum cites the founder's autobiography for its version, the heritage site and Omroep Brabant call theirs tradition, and none gives a date.
Kalff worked with the young architect Leo de Bever, who lived from 1930 to 2015.
Brabants Erfgoed calls Kalff an already retired artistic adviser to the Philips board.
The Philips Museum gives a different picture, since it lists him as head of Philips Design until 1960 and still active in the project.
The two descriptions are compatible, because a man can leave a post and stay an adviser.

The name came from the exhibition expert Jacques Kleiboer, the museum says, who meant it as an essentially optimistic concept. The physicist Jan F. Schouten supplied the philosophy: a show of the relationship between people and technology, dynamic and looking ahead, not a catalog of products. The museum adds that 120 company specialists worked in 18 groups, and that the English exhibition designer James Gardner was brought in.
The building went up between 1962 and 1966, according to the heritage news site De Erfgoedstem.
Prince Bernhard and Frits Philips opened it on September 24, 1966.

blocks.x: What the saucer is made of

r: The numbers are consistent across sources, and I give them here once. The dish has a diameter of 77 meters and the building is almost 32 meters high. It rests on twelve V-shaped column pairs, which Omroep Brabant counts as 24 columns.

The Dutch architecture database describes two shells on twelve 8-meter V-shaped columns around a glass entrance hall, 48 windows in the rim of the upper shell, an 8-meter plexiglass skylight, a shell built from 822 hexagonal concrete elements of 1,200 kilograms each, ring-shaped steel cables with a combined length of 169 kilometers, and a total weight of 15,000 tons. It gives 6,000 square meters of exhibition space reached by a hydraulic lift with a glass shaft, and a 60-meter concrete mast beside the building.
A 2026 profile in a regional magazine repeats these figures and adds that the pond in the park has the same 77-meter diameter as the dish.
Some of the park was never built as drawn. The artists Constant, Volten, Haber and Clough designed the park, and Philips rejected their design.
The architecture database says so, and the 2026 profile agrees.

blocks.x: Half a million visitors a year

r: The numbers on visitors come as three different kinds of figure. The Philips Museum says the millionth visitor arrived on November 21, 1968.
Omroep Brabant gives 527,000 visitors in the peak year 1970 and an average of 475,000 a year until 1980.
Brabants Erfgoed says about ten million visitors had been counted when the Evoluon closed to the public in 1989.
Next Nature's own page says "over 500,000 visitors by 1970," which could be read as a cumulative figure, and Omroep Brabant's yearly figure shows it was one year's count.
Taken together the figures fit: a million by late 1968, a peak year near 527,000 and a lifetime total near ten million.
Visitors turned knobs and ran experiments, which the Philips Museum says was new to the Netherlands and was imitated by later science centers such as NEMO in Amsterdam.
A 2026 profile by a former student worker adds details such as a counter of four red tubes in the hall that tracked the number of people inside, and a fire-code cap of 2,000 visitors at once.
That is one person's memory in a magazine, and I treat it as color and not as a measurement.

blocks.x: Closed in 1989, and what came after

r: Sources give different reasons for the closure. The Philips Museum says it was no longer justifiable for Philips to carry the high operating costs.
Omroep Brabant says the museum became too expensive.
Next Nature's page says declining visitor numbers and changing views on science communication.
Those readings are compatible, since a costly museum with falling attendance is hard to defend. They share one claim, which is that the company stopped.
After 1989 the building became a closed reception center for Philips and later a congress center, according to Omroep Brabant.
The architecture database says congress use dates from 1994 and that new buildings were added on the 5.8-hectare site.
A magazine profile says an auditorium was built next to the building.

The year the congress function began is not settled in the sources I could open, and English-language references give other years. In January 1994 the city's executive board designated the building a municipal monument, as NOS recalled in 2018.

The record shows temporary life in the building as well. A regional magazine says the first temporary exhibition, about the human brain, was organized in 2012, and the German band Kraftwerk played there in 2013.
The tourist board counts four concerts.

The heritage status rose in 2018. NOS reported on February 20, 2018 that the municipality had announced the Evoluon was designated a national monument, and that the city's earlier municipal status would be withdrawn.
The trade site Architectenweb adds that the decision was the minister's, Ingrid van Engelshoven's, and De Erfgoedstem, a day later, calls the building an icon of the postwar rebuilding period.
NOS also reported one idea floated that year, to place a national design museum in the building.

blocks.x: Sold by Philips, effective January 1, 2019

r: The building was not the city's property in the way the word gift suggests. The tourist board writes that Philips gifted the Evoluon to the city for the company's 75th anniversary, and Omroep Brabant calls it a present from Philips to the city.
But on December 20, 2018 Innovation Origins reported that the combination Hurks, Foolen & Reijs would become the new owner on January 1, 2019, "the current owner" being Philips.
I read the gift as a gift in spirit to the citizens, with ownership staying with Philips for 52 years.

The report describes a process Philips started in the fall of 2017. Fifteen parties applied, seven presented plans in the summer, and a committee led by the president of Philips Nederland chose the Eindhoven partnership of Foolen & Reijs Vastgoed and Hurks vastgoedontwikkeling. A new Evoluon Foundation was to program the building, with Philips as a member. Philips and the buyers agreed a clause against speculation, a chain clause against splitting up the site, and an intention to make the Evoluon available free for at least half the time for technology, design, education and culture. Renovation and the new program were to start in the summer of 2021, and the tenant Regus stayed until then.
The buyers' own vision text says the icon would reopen to the public in 2021 with a park around it.

The price is less well documented. A heritage trade site, writing in January 2021, says the building was sold in 2018 for 4.2 million euros, a relatively modest sum, on condition it become accessible again.
I found no second source for the figure.

blocks.x: Next Nature moves in

r: In September 2020 the TU/e campus paper reported that the national government would release 2 million euros over four years for a futurelab for design and technology, led by Koert van Mensvoort of Next Nature, with the Evoluon as its planned home. It quotes him planning a first project in 2021 and a complete futurelab by 2025, and it names Jan Mengelers, president of the Evoluon Foundation, as the contact.
The paper notes that the plan had first lost out to Waag in the Council for Culture's advice and was rescued by a motion in the House.

On June 30, 2021 Next Nature announced that its plans had received 7.6 million euros from the Region Deal Brainport Eindhoven. From January 1, 2022 it would be the new crew of the monument, and it named Lichtstad Erfgoed as the owner it works with.

The announcement does not say how Lichtstad Erfgoed relates to the buyers named in 2018, and I did not find a register entry that links the names. In the fall of 2021 Next Nature turned the building into a virtual reality time machine, and it planned a full reopening from 2025.

The public reopening came in stages, and on September 24, 2022, fifty-six years to the day after the opening, the building reopened with RetroFuture, which KIVI says used 3,000 square meters on four rings.
Next Nature describes ten tunnels of fiction and facts, with works by Studio Drift, Driessens & Verstappen and others, and funding from several cultural funds and public bodies.

The interior studio M+R says its brief was to restore the monument's clarity with limited means. It cut visual clutter, painted existing furnishings in one blue and filled the public rooms with chairs by designers from Eindhoven and Brabant such as Maarten Baas and Piet Hein Eek, each item labeled for auction after use.

The plan Next Nature published for the full building divides the story into four rings: the origin of the universe and Earth, the origin of life, technology as a force on the planet, and the visitor's own role as crew of what it calls spaceship Earth.
The original exhibition space is described elsewhere as three rings, so the fourth ring may be Next Nature's own count.
By summer 2024, a regional magazine says, only the building was called Evoluon and the museum was the Next Nature Museum.

blocks.x: Dutch Design Week, from 2022

r: The archive question has a clear answer from Dutch public broadcaster VPRO's tips for DDW 2022, which says the Evoluon is a DDW location for the first time that year.

That explains why the photo archive has no earlier Evoluon album, and I found no evidence that DDW used the building before. The 2017 album titled HUBOT, which I could not place before, belongs elsewhere: Next Nature's own page says HUBOT was at the MediaMarkt in Eindhoven during DDW 2017.

The 2022 album holds 22 photos. Six are credited to about.today and show a person in a virtual reality headset, and 16 are credited to Tommy Köhlbrugge and titled West_Evoluon_RetroFuture, dated October 22 and 23, 2022.
The 2023 album holds 13 photos by about.today dated October 20, 2023, showing geodesic domes.

The domes belong to Spacefarming: the future of food, which Next Nature says ran from September 2023 until July 2025, with a list of 28 names that includes SPACE10, Solar Foods, Wageningen University & Research and the European Space Agency.
A design press story from 2023 describes domes housing lab-grown meat substitutes and an insect-powered cookbook.
The 2024 album holds seven photos by Köhlbrugge, dated October 19 to 23.

DDW's recap of the West area names Microbial Oasis, A House of Salt, Meet Meat: Rourou's Adventure and a Breathing Session with Geoffrey Lillemon, and the album shows a breathing session on the floor.
Spacefarming was still on view, which is consistent with the algae dome in the album.
The 2025 album holds 14 photos by Almicheal Fraay, and it includes a blue reception desk that fits M+R's blue scheme.
DDW listed a Digital & AI hub called Digital Futures with 31 presentations at the Next Nature Museum, whose entrance DDW lists as partially paid.
Next Nature's annual report adds the Next Nature Conference 2025 on bio design and a Design Debate on Saturday, October 25 in the Philips Hall, led by Tracy Metz and Wouter van Noort.

For 2026, DDW's page for the Next Nature Museum lists nine opening days from October 17 to 25, with 11:00 to 18:00 shown for October 17, partly paid entry, and four items. Quantum Safari Game is an exhibition of six interactive quantum installations by Next Nature and QDNL, open all week.
A symposium on the creative economy with Peter Wennink among the speakers is listed for Monday, October 19.
The National Design Debate 2026, titled Shaping Europe, takes place in the Philips Hall on Friday, October 23, and Waag announced a three-year partnership with the museum to hold it.
A conference called PROMPT, on AI as an artistic material, is listed as well.

blocks.x: A new future on view almost every year

r: The program titles show what the building keeps updating. In 2022 the future on view was the past's version of it, in RetroFuture. From 2023 to 2025 it was food, in Spacefarming. At DDW 2025 it was digital life and AI, and in 2026 DDW lists quantum physics and a debate on European design.
That is a reading of titles and not of the exhibitions themselves, which I did not see. It does match the principle in the Philips Museum's account: a show about technology that does not stand still.

The cost of that principle appears in the annual report for 2025. Paying visitors rose from 54,837 in 2023 to 62,651 in 2024 and 76,636 in 2025, and the museum aims for 150,000 visitors a year by 2030. The report also records a loss of 168,514.50 euros in 2025, the first red figures in the organization's history, multi-year commitments of more than a million euros a year from the state, province and municipality for 2025 to 2028, building costs of about the same size, and a park development that was taking longer than hoped.
On the park, the landscape studio LOLA says the city commissioned a framework for a 15-hectare park, and that the council approved plans that include two new buildings with affordable housing.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: The gift framing says the city, and the sales report names Philips as the owner until January 1, 2019. The sales report is the later and more specific document, and I use it.
Twelve V-shaped columns in one source and 24 columns in another. They describe the same structure, twelve V-shaped pairs.
Lunch, dinner, menu card. Not settled, and the versions differ.
The original exhibition space is described as three rings, and both KIVI and Next Nature's plan speak of four. I cannot tell whether the fourth is the top ring or a count Next Nature made for itself.
Next Nature's page reads as a total and Omroep Brabant's as one year. Omroep Brabant's yearly figure fits the other totals.
Whether DDW used the building before 2022.
VPRO's statement and the absence of earlier albums agree.
Next Nature places it at a store, not at the Evoluon.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know when the congress function began, whether in 1989 or 1994 or in between, and I found no Philips document that says.
I do not know how Lichtstad Erfgoed relates to Hurks, Foolen & Reijs, or the price of the 2018 sale, which rests on one trade report.
I do not know why Kalff's sketch story varies, or which meal it was.

I cannot say what the visitors to the 2022 to 2025 DDW exhibitions saw beyond what the program texts and album titles say, and I read the Flickr albums on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen them for this version.

If you visit during Dutch Design Week 2026, look at what the building asks you to imagine and when that vision was first proposed. Which of today's futures on show do you expect a visitor to find quaint in thirty years, and which do you expect to hold up?

posts.title: Hallenweg is a street of workshops, and the archive follows its tenants
posts.subtitle: A post-war row of business halls in Eindhoven, the design area that took its name, and seven editions of the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Hallenweg: a street, a DDW area and its tenants
posts.description: Hallenweg in Eindhoven from post-war halls to a Dutch Design Week area that now reaches beyond the street, with what the records do and do not show.

r: Hallenweg is a street of post-war business halls, and by 2026 the Dutch Design Week area that carries its name reaches well beyond the street.

That sentence is easy to miss if you read the archive the way the archive is filed. The photo albums say Hallenweg, Vij5, Jeroen Wand or Atelier NL, and a reader could take all four for neighbors on one street.

The sources I opened say something more careful: the street is one place, the DDW area is another, and the tenants who made the area known have moved around inside it and out of it. This essay uses public sources only: the tourist board, a heritage news item, DDW's area recaps, location pages and program items, the studios' own pages and the DDW photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview.

blocks.x: A post-war scheme for small industry

r: The tourist board's roundup of Eindhoven's design areas says Hallenweg came into being after the Second World War as an economic recovery project. It says the first tenants were mostly metal and welding firms, that the buildings were constructed in the style of the Delft School, and that they are hidden behind the Hoogstraat.
That is the whole published description I could open. It gives no architect and no date.

The city's own history page sets the scene. The war left Eindhoven damaged, with the Philips factories bombed and the Demer shopping street destroyed in the bombing of December 6, 1942, and afterward the city rebuilt quickly and became the fastest-growing city in the Netherlands, with a housing shortage, a ring road and new districts in Woensel and Gestel.
A scheme of halls for small industry fits that period, though the city's page does not mention Hallenweg.

DDW's 2026 pages repeat the story with one more detail. The Hal2 location page says Hallenweg was originally built as part of the city's post-war reconstruction in 1951, and the Muziek&Ko page, for Hallenweg 7, says it was built after the war as an economic recovery project in the Delft School style and keeps its industrial character.
The 1951 date is DDW's own, and I could not check it against the city's monument file.

A heritage news item of January 9, 2016 adds the status of the halls. Eindhoven had designated seven new buildings from the reconstruction period as municipal monuments, out of 24 that the city's executive board had proposed in 2014, and the item lists the business halls at Hallenweg 1 to 7c among them. The other 17 were to be decided in March or April.
The same list of seven includes the power station at Strijp-T on Beukenlaan.

That may be why the two places get linked, because they appear together in a single municipal decision. The tourist board still lists Strijp-T and Hallenweg as separate entries, and I found no source that places Hallenweg inside the Strijp-T area.

I could not read the city's own monument file. The city's monument dossier host answered with a rejection page when I asked for it, and I did not try again, so the register's architect and construction year stay out of this essay.

blocks.x: Metal shops first, then studios

r: The street's present life shows up in tenants' own words. The interior design-and-build company Hal2 says it started twenty years ago at Hallenweg 2, the second hall, and has now grown into a renovated Hallenweg 3. The page is undated, and I read "twenty years" as relative to its writing.

In October 2015 Innovation Origins described the workspace of the designer Jeroen Wand on Hallenweg, with a large outdoor area, chickens outside and a radio inside. It said his newest work would be shown in the studio during DDW 2015, alongside guests including Jo Sijen and Wouter Corvers, and listed his Phases vases among the pieces.
Vij5 describes itself as a publisher of design products, and its own site gives a studio, workshop and showroom address in Den Bosch.
DDW's program for 2021 says Vij5 was celebrating its fifteenth birthday, and the DDW 2026 listing for its anniversary show is titled "20 jaar Vij5," which puts the label's start around 2006.
A designer interview on Vij5's site says Wand settled in Eindhoven when a friend found a studio too big for one person, and that his studio now has several employees.

blocks.x: DDW's own pages, year by year

r: DDW's recap of 2018, which says the festival has eight design areas, tells visitors that the designers of the Hallenweg welcome them in their studios. It names Vij5 with a project called Kies Kleur, in which the public chooses a color, and it lists Jeroen Wand and Maarten Baptist as exhibitors. Atelier NL appears with the sentence that the church of Atelier NL is just a stone's throw away, and the recap adds that Atelier NL was the previous year's ambassador of Dutch Design Week.
The recap says "a stone's throw away," which places the church near the street and not on it.

In 2019, now counting nine areas, DDW's recap sends visitors to Vij5, which showed the origins of its collection, to Atelier NL's church for an indoor forest, and to a ceramics presentation called Arita. It also names Studio van der Zandt and an enormous coin track called 50/50 by the agency HeyHeyDeHaas.

A design site's 2019 report places the area in the south-west of the festival map and describes it as private studios opened to the public, with projects on interaction, sustainability and ceramic craft combined with technology.

In 2021 the area preview, back at eight areas with Hallenweg marked G on the map, lists Vij5's anniversary candles, Atelier NL's natural-materials exhibitions including a flax project and a water school, and two shows at De Fabriek.

The 2024 recap says the hidden gems of Dutch Design Week are in the Hallenweg area, and it names De Fabriek with Polluted Plants to Pottery and (w)aardewerk, Studio Jeroen Wand with Stacking and EXO, and Atelier NL's Meanderende Maas and a dinner called Smaak van de Bodem in the Atelier NL church.
Vij5 says in a blog post that its 2024 exhibition, Introducing Tomorrow, could be found in its workshop on Hallenweg, with six new and four renewed designs.
I found area recaps titled for 2021 and 2022 as videos with no text I could read, and none for 2023 or 2025.

blocks.x: What seven editions of photographs show

r: The official archive holds Hallenweg-related albums for seven editions: 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020 and 2024. Together they hold 11 albums and 143 photos.

The 2015 album has 18 photos by Ralph Roelse with number titles, showing a courtyard with Studio Jeroen Wand signs, a shipping container and workshop rooms with ceramics and pendant lamps. In 2016 the archive splits the street into two albums: 7 photos of Wand's workshop by Iris Rijskamp and 39 of Vij5 whose titles read "image by Vij5," meaning the label supplied them. In 2017 and 2018 each studio again has an album, and Rijskamp took all of them. The 2019 album of Vij5 has 5 photos and the 2020 album has 30, credited in the titles I read to Max Kneefel. The 2024 album has 5 photos by Anwyn Howarth and is titled Atelier NL (Hallenweg), showing a mound of earth among tables of ceramics.

The archive follows the tenants. The street name appears in album titles in 2015, 2016, 2017 and 2024, and after 2017 the albums are named for the studio. I cannot say from the titles that the 2019 and 2020 Vij5 albums were photographed on the street.

blocks.x: The label travels

r: DDW's 2026 location pages show how far the area label has stretched. The Dutch locations page lists, under the Hallenweg area, Atelier Fig. at Hallenweg 11, Atelier NL at Bergmannstraat 76, De Fabriek at Baarsstraat 38, Design Daily's at Gestelsestraat 234, Hal2 at Hallenweg 3, Muziek & Ko at Hallenweg 7, Studio Jeroen Wand at Bayeuxlaan 7 and Studio Tast at Gestelsestraat 238.
DDW's 2026 pages give a flavor of the area's tenants. Muziek&Ko at Hallenweg 7 shows Design by Resonance, instruments shaped by sound, with workshops and live music.
Atelier Fig shows its Fringe technique in an industrial warehouse that the page says was made available by a natural stone specialist.
De Fabriek lists a group exhibition of master projects from two LUCA schools in Belgium among its items, and Studio Tast invites visitors to test neuro-inclusive solutions for education and work.
Teun Zwets is on Hallenweg itself: the DDW page says his studio found a new home in early 2026, with workshop, showroom, office and canteen under one roof, and a show of 50 chairs.
Wand's page gives Bayeuxlaan 7, in the Hallenweg area and not on the street, where in 2015 his workspace was on Hallenweg.
Atelier NL's own site gives Bergmannstraat 76 as its address, and DDW's 2026 page says it is situated in the former Bergmann Church on Bergmannstraat.

So the church counts as part of the Hallenweg area on DDW's map and as a neighbor of the street in the 2018 recap, and it is not on Hallenweg. The 2024 album title "Atelier NL (Hallenweg)" reads as the area label.
Vij5 is the other change. Its 2026 anniversary show is listed under the Canal area at APTUM, in the NRE site, at Gashouder 13, not in the Hallenweg area.
That does not mean Vij5 has left the street for good, and I found no 2026 source that says where its workshop is.
For October 17 to 25, 2026, DDW lists the Teun Zwets and Wand shows as free and open from 11:00 to 18:00 on the first day.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: The tourist board lists Hallenweg and Strijp-T as separate areas. The municipal monument decision of January 2016 lists both, which is likely why they get linked. I use the tourist board's listing for the areas.

The 2018 recap says near the street, Atelier NL's own site says Bergmannstraat 76, and DDW's 2026 list says the same address under the Hallenweg area. These agree once the area is separated from the street.

Vij5 describes a studio, workshop and showroom in Den Bosch, while its 2024 blog places an exhibition in a workshop on Hallenweg. Both can be true if the festival showroom and the base are different places, and that is my reading.
DDW said eight in 2018, nine in 2019 and eight in 2021. The recaps do not say what changed.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know who designed the halls at Hallenweg 1 to 7c or when they were built. The tourist board names a style and the heritage news item gives a status, and neither gives an architect or a year.
I do not know when DDW first used the street, why 2021 to 2023 and 2025 have no album, or whether the 2019 and 2020 Vij5 albums show Hallenweg.
I do not know where Vij5's workshop stands in 2026, and I did not find an exhibitor list for the area in 2025.

If you walk the area during DDW 2026, you could try the archive's test on a studio door. Does the sign name the street, the studio, or only the work, and which of those would still tell a reader where they were ten years from now?

posts.title: A power plant for Philips factories, now a stage for design questions about AI
posts.subtitle: The Innovation Powerhouse in Eindhoven, from a Philips energy plant of the 1950s to a design and technology building, followed through planning, press and Dutch Design Week records
posts.seoTitle: Innovation Powerhouse: a Philips power plant reborn
posts.description: The Innovation Powerhouse in Eindhoven from Philips energy plant TR to a Dutch Design Week venue, with what the records do and do not show.

r: The Innovation Powerhouse was built to make power for Philips factories, and Dutch Design Week now lists it as a place where design asks questions about AI.

I like a building whose first job is on the record, because it gives me something firm to hold while the exhibitions change. This essay draws on public sources only: an architecture and planning record, the city's image bank, trade press, the building's developers and architects, Dutch Design Week's pages and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview.

blocks.x: A power plant that grew in stages

r: The Eindhoven architecture center's walking guide, published in January 2021, says the energy plant TR was born at the start of the 1950s on the drawing boards of Philips's own Architects and Engineers Bureau. It was delivered with a single chimney, and the second chimney, like the first 76 meters high, dates from 1953. The plant was extended in 1956 and 1960, and the turbine hall was extended in 1970. Over those years it burned coal, then oil and finally natural gas.

Other sources compress the same history into four stages. The firm that supplied the windows for the conversion and the Dutch architecture site Architectuur.nl both say the plant was built in four phases between 1953 and 1972 and supplied the Philips factories on Strijp R, S and T. Architectuur.nl places the turbines and generators in the low volume, the coal transport and storage in the narrow high-rise, and the steam boilers in a third volume to the north, while Reynaers puts the steam boilers in the high volume.
Both name the architect of the 1953 design as C. Last.
The architecture site urbanNext gives the same 1953 to 1972 span.

One source gives an earlier year. A story on the city's image bank says that in 1951 Philips built its own coal-fired power station on the Zwaanstraat to meet growing demand, that the coal came by a rail line crossing the Beukenlaan, and that a viaduct was built so traffic and freight trains could pass. It adds that in the 1960s, when the Netherlands moved to natural gas, the plant was converted to gas and the coal line lost its function.
The 1951 date and the 1953 design date are not the same milestone, and I cannot tell from the pages which is the earlier stage of one project. I use "the early 1950s" and name the sources.

The wider site had its own history. The same walking guide says Philips owned the Strijp-T land before the war but developed it only after it, with a carton factory and a paper factory as the first large buildings, designed by Philips's bureau.

blocks.x: The spine that was never finished

r: The plant's silhouette was meant to be symmetrical. The coal chutes in the narrow central high-rise were built in the third phase, and in 1972 the owners decided to build only the lower volume that was needed, so the 1953 design stayed unfinished.
The reason, the sources agree, was the change of fuel: coal chutes were no longer needed.
The 2018 conversion completed the silhouette with a steel frame that holds terraces, a glass elevator, emergency stairs and a vertical garden, and a glass extension on the other side.
The five-meter-wide middle section still has concrete coal chutes hanging at a height of 28 meters.
The conversion was nominated for the Dirk Roosenburg prize in 2019, and since 2020 the chimneys have carried a light artwork, according to the architecture center.

blocks.x: A municipal building, then a private conversion

r: Ownership changed in the middle of the story. Reynaers, whose aluminum profiles were used in the conversion, says the building belonged to the municipality from 2011, and after an asbestos remediation by the municipality, a remediation company and the developer Geva Vastgoed, the municipality sold it to Geva for redevelopment.

Ad van Berlo, founder of the design agency VanBerlo, told the Eindhoven IO+ archive in July 2015 that he looked up the first photograph he took of the plant, dated March 9, 2011, that the building was full of asbestos and unfit to work in, and that he expected it to host his agency and about ten other innovative companies in two years.

The same architecture sources say he asked the architect Margriet Eugelink in 2011 to study how such a program could fit, and that in 2015 Geva commissioned three architects, Janne van Berlo of Atelier Van Berlo, Eugelink and Stefan de Bever, to design the transformation.
Two openings appear in the record. IO+ wrote in May 2019 that Van Berlo could finally celebrate the official opening of the building in September 2017.

A Strijp-T news item written at the move-in says that VanBerlo had moved into the former plant, that public visitors had to wait, and that the official opening of the Innovation Powerhouse would take place during Dutch Design Week, with a first exhibition on the ground floor between the concrete pillars titled Chronic Health: Designing a Healthy Future.
The first looks like the opening of VanBerlo's own offices and the second like the opening to the public. That is my reading and neither source says it.

The architecture site says the VanBerlo office covers 2,300 square meters around a two-story atrium, and that the atrium's wooden stairs served as a tribune at presentations and for television recordings of De Toekomstbouwers during DDW 2018.

An organizer's page says the 2018 exhibition belonged to an Embassy of Health, organized by Waag, VanBerlo, Philips, Maxima Medical Center and U Create, and called Chronic Health: If not then Who?, an open lab for care applications.

A municipal listing has protected the plant since 2016. A heritage news item of January 9, 2016 names the energy plant Strijp-TR on Beukenlaan among seven new municipal monuments from the reconstruction period, in the same decision that listed the Hallenweg halls.
The plant is a typical example of reconstruction-period factory architecture, according to the architecture site.

blocks.x: Tenants, and a district around it

r: IO+ reported in February 2018 that the owner of Strijp-T, the real estate company Geva, was recruiting companies, and that earlier users of the site such as Smurfit Kappa and Draka had moved in after Philips gradually left. It said a new phase had started with the arrival of VanBerlo the year before.

In May 2019 IO+ said the power plant, now called Innovation Powerhouse, was fully rented, with the buildings behind it also let. It named VanBerlo, Additive Industries, CTOUCH, Amber and Thermo Fisher Scientific among the companies on the site, and Ad van Berlo as chair of the first board of a new foundation to connect them.

The site around the plant describes itself in strong terms. IO+ in February 2018 called Strijp-T the terrain Philips developed right after Strijp-S, said spin-offs such as NXP and ASML emerged there, and called it the birthplace of the Brainport region, and its 2019 report adds that the cd and the dvd were invented there.

Those are promotional claims in trade press and I have not checked them against a Philips source. The same 2018 report says the fence around the 27-hectare site, a standard feature in Philips times, was slowly disappearing.

VanBerlo is now part of Accenture. Accenture's press release of February 19, 2020 says it had acquired the Eindhoven-based agency, which then had more than 90 professionals in Eindhoven and The Hague and joined Accenture's Industry X.0 practice.

That helps explain why Accenture's design teams are the repeat host in DDW's pages for this building. DDW names Accenture Industry X | Industrial Design in 2023, Accenture Industrial Design in 2025 and Accenture in 2026.
No page I opened lists the building's other current tenants.

blocks.x: Dutch Design Week, year by year

r: The earliest DDW-related record I found for this place is 2018, with the Chronic Health exhibition and the official opening described above.

In 2019, in a piece on its nine design areas dated October 25, 2019, DDW sent visitors to the Innovation Powerhouse "formerly the Philips power plant" to see the Embassy of Sustainable Design and noted the TQ building behind it.
I found no DDW page for the building in 2020, 2021, 2022 or 2024.

In 2023 DDW lists The Language of Sustainability, presented by Accenture Industry X | Industrial Design. Its text says storytelling and visual thinking help designers see how ecology, sociopolitical systems and products connect, and it names TU Delft with a project on composite material waste and two Accenture projects, Wings for Aid and Designing Sustainable North Stars.
The page prints no location. So I cannot say from it that the exhibition stood in this building, and I do not caption a 2023 photograph with its title unless a sign does.

The archive of the DDW Flickr account holds an album titled Innovation Powerhouse for 2023 with 13 photos, all by Tommy Köhlbrugge, with titles dated October 21, 24 and 26, 2023. I see a hall of raw concrete with a large folded cardboard drone under a sign that reads Wings For Aid, a white model plane hanging from wires, glass domes with small objects and a courtyard with colored chairs in front of container huts.
Wings for Aid is one of the Accenture projects DDW lists for the exhibition.

For 2025 DDW names the building. Accenture Industrial Design hosted an exhibition called Designing Interaction with Physical AI at Strijp T+R, Innovation Powerhouse, free of charge, from October 18 to 26, 2025, 11:00 to 18:00.
The text asks what changes when everyday products begin to perceive, learn and respond, and it picks the kitchen as the place to test that, a room it calls one of the most human spaces of all.

Those are the host's questions, and the page gives no result. The 2025 album has 7 photos by Almicheal Fraay of a kitchen island with a hob, visitors around it and a black panel with the exhibition title.
For 2026, DDW's location page lists Zwaanstraat 31a, open 11:00 to 18:00 on October 17 and daily to October 25, and links an Accenture item called The Hornet Trap: Designing for Living Systems.

Its text describes a smart trap meant to target the invasive yellow-legged hornet while limiting harm to native insects, developed with the Arvespa Foundation and informed by beekeepers, with a prototype as the starting point.
I have not seen this exhibit and nobody should read this essay as a review of it.

blocks.x: What a thin record can still teach

r: Across the years the host's questions change. In 2018 the question was health care and open design, in 2019 sustainability, in 2023 storytelling for sustainability, in 2025 physical AI in the kitchen and in 2026 technology that protects biodiversity.
That pattern comes from the program texts, and it is a pattern of titles. The photographs fit it only loosely.

The building history and the program pages come from different kinds of source, and each answers a different question. A power plant that supplied Philips factories tells me what the walls were made for. A program page tells me what a host wanted visitors to think. The archive photographs show what a camera saw on certain days. A caption that mixes the three without saying so will claim more than any one of them can support.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: The city image bank says a coal power station was built in 1951, while the architecture sources date the design and the second chimney to 1953 and the plant's four phases to 1953 to 1972. Not settled.
IO+ gives September 2017 for the official opening, and the Strijp-T item places the official opening in DDW 2018. These can be two events.
The program page prints no address and the photo album carries the building's name. The album settles where the photographs were taken and not the exhibition's title.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know the exact date the plant stopped operating, and I did not find a document that says so. The building sources describe it as no longer used for power, and a plant to its west is described as still operating.
I do not know who owns the building today or who all its tenants are.
I do not know why the archive has albums only for 2023 and 2025, whether DDW 2024 had a program in the building, or what the 2026 exhibit looks like inside.

If you open one of its albums, write down the year, then look for any sign, label or title that names an exhibit before you decide what you are looking at. Which of the two lists would you trust more in a caption: the one from the wall, or the one from the program?
