posts.title: MU Hybrid Art House: a radio factory, a Japanese character and twelve Octobers of Dutch Design Week
posts.subtitle: An Eindhoven art house followed through the national monument register, its own exhibition archive and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
posts.seoTitle: MU Hybrid Art House: radio factory to art house
posts.description: MU Hybrid Art House on Strijp-S, from a Philips radio factory to Dutch Design Week shows, with what its own archive and the register do and do not say.

r: MU Hybrid Art House has occupied the ground floor of a former Philips radio factory on Strijp-S since 2013, and its exhibition archive shows what it put in that building each autumn since.

This essay uses public sources only: MU's own pages and exhibition archive, the national monument register, Dutch government and housing-corporation pages, press coverage and the official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview. MU's current website loads its text with scripts and is hard to read, but its older website still holds the full exhibition archive, and that archive settles several questions that look open elsewhere. I say below which source settled each one.

I also have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was for before I ask what it is now. A building that made radios and now makes arguments about artificial intelligence is a fair test of that habit.

blocks.x: MU began in 1998 and carries a Zen word

r: MU describes its own history in a short text on its website. It says MU began in 1998 in De Witte Dame, a former Philips factory in the center of Eindhoven, as a merger of several small initiatives in visual art, architecture, pop culture and design.
It has belonged to the national cultural infrastructure since 2005, as a small presentation institution until 2012 and as a large one since.

A 2023 interview in Brabant Cultureel adds the people. It says the director and artistic leader, Angelique Spaninks, took over in 2005 from Ton van Gool, who started MU in 1998 as a place where, at the initiative of the municipality of Eindhoven, several small initiatives in visual art, design, architecture and pop culture were to come together. Spaninks says in that interview that she built on his lines and added bio art and design, engaged art, digital media and performance. The same article says she came to MU from the regional newspaper Eindhovens Dagblad.
The name is explained on MU's About page. It comes from a Japanese character that stands for synergy, and in Zen the term goes beyond either-or thinking and leaves room to postpone judgment.
The Brabant Cultureel article renders the same character as nothing or emptiness and adds the sentence that anything can arise from nothing.
I note both readings because the character is used differently in different places, and MU's own text chooses synergy.
MU has three stated pillars: public presentations, talent development and education.

Its 2017 to 2020 activity plan, which the Cultuur Eindhoven foundation publishes, adds numbers. It says MU's projects drew about 40,000 to 90,000 physical visitors a year, with Dutch Design Week and Glow Next named as the peaks. It reports 105,098 digital sessions by 78,207 unique visitors on MU's websites in 2015, against 70,807 sessions by 53,603 unique visitors in 2013.
Those are the organization's own figures and I have found no later ones.

blocks.x: The building: a radio factory on the Hoge Rug

r: Which building is MU in? The answer is on MU's old news page. It announced that MU was turning 15 and opening a second space on Strijp-S: one thousand square meters on the ground floor of the building called Gerard, at Torenallee 40-06, with an opening party on Saturday, May 18.

The page carries no year. MU was founded in 1998, so its 15th birthday is in 2013, and May 18, 2013 was a Saturday. That date arithmetic is mine, and it matches the year MU gives for its move in every other text.
One source disagrees. The housing corporation Trudo, which redeveloped the building, says on its project page that the art space MU was established there in 2014.

MU's own archive explains how both can be right. It lists five shows in a series called MUtate from February to June 2014, and a Studio LONK project page describes MU's last five months in De Witte Dame as a monthly relay of artists before the move to Strijp-S, without a year.

I read that as the Strijp-S space opening in May 2013 and the old home closing in mid-2014. I have not seen a source that says so in one sentence, and a 2014 local news item about the farewell exhibition turned up in a search but could not be opened, so that part is second-hand.

Gerard and its neighbor Anton are two of the Philips radio-factory buildings on the Hoge Rug, a row of concrete production buildings at Strijp-S. A building survey for the municipality, written by a firm of building historians, says a new radio factory took over most of the site from the mid-1920s and that the concrete production buildings SK (1927), SAN (1929) and SBP (1930) still stand.

The national register lists these three as one rijksmonument, number 518771, registered on February 16, 2004, with a design credited to the Philips engineer A. de Broekert, and the address list for that monument includes Torenallee 40-06 itself. The register adds that the interiors have changed greatly through changed use.

So MU's building is a national monument, which matters because the Dutch government's transformation database says the monument status restricted the conversion and that uncertainty about the restrictions raised its cost.

That database, from the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO), also records what the work was. The former radio factories SAN (Anton) and SBP (Gerard) became 276 lofts plus commercial space, finished in 2013, with an address range of Torenallee 30 to 60 and an original construction year of 1927 for the project.
Trudo says all 276 lofts were let and that it placed the art space on the ground floor because public functions belong there.
Here the sources split, and I cannot settle it. RVO says Gerard is the former SBP. A French database of architecture says Gerard is the former SAN and dates it to 1929.
The register entry does not label the three buildings by name.

If RVO is right, MU's building went up in 1930, and if the French database is right, in 1929. I lean to RVO because it is a government record, but a government page can carry the same error as a database, and I did not find the primary drawing or permit that would settle it.

blocks.x: Strijp-S: a fenced city that opened in the 2000s

r: The site's own owners tell a short history. Strijp-S's website says Philips had its first factory built there in 1916, a glass factory making bulbs for lamps, and that the company became self-sufficient on the site, from raw material to finished product. It says the area was called the Forbidden City because it was fenced and you needed a pass, and that about 10,000 people worked there in the 1970s.
The national register gives the same starting point from the heritage side: a need for its own glass factory during the First World War started the new complex.
The sale date needs care because sources differ. Strijp-S's history page says 2002, when VolkerWessels and the municipality of Eindhoven bought the site from Philips and leased it back for a time.
A German architecture trade site says production stopped and the site was sold in 2004.

I trust the site owner's own history over a trade summary, and I did not find a deed. The Strijp-S page also says Dutch Design Week chose the area as its new home after the first buildings opened up, and that the Klokgebouw and the Glasgebouw led the redevelopment.

blocks.x: What the archive shows, year by year

r: The official DDW photo archive on Flickr holds MU albums for 2015 to 2022, 2024 and 2025, ten editions and 658 photos by my October 6 count. I could not reopen Flickr for this pass, so every count and photographer credit below comes from that earlier reading and stays second-hand.
What changed is that MU's own exhibition archive now lets me say what was on show in each of those Octobers.

The album is titled Collective [Ir]Rationality. MU's page says it ran from October 5 to 25, 2015, and was a spatial installation by Studio KNOL on the herd behavior of festival crowds. It says that MU had been visited by more than 36,000 people in nine days during the previous year's DDW.
That is the only DDW-week visitor count for MU that I found.
For Play, Shaping Sexuality ran from October 7 to November 13, 2016, curated by Sanne Muiser and Tom Loois, with more than 30 invited artists and designers.

The same page lists the other things MU did in DDW week: a daily design talk show called Create Out Loud, an art-book pop-up shop and The Parliament of Things, which it places at the MU container at Plug-In-City.

That settles where the Parliament of Things stood: at a container, and not in the building. The archive's 24 photographs under that title therefore show the container. MU's activity plan says it had managed two containers at Plug In City since 2015 as an outside presentation and development space.
I leave the content of For Play at its title, because the show deals with adult themes and nothing in this essay depends on it.
Materialising the Internet ran from October 6 to November 12, 2017, curated by Nadine Roestenburg and Spaninks, with more than 20 international artists and designers.
The artists listed include Joey Holder, who appears again in 2025 as the maker of Ambiogenesis.
The New Newsroom, subtitled Reporting Redesigned, ran from October 12 to November 11, 2018, under the same two curators, with a newsroom set up inside the exhibition.
Domus, the Italian design magazine, called it the most interesting show of that DDW and confirms the closing date.

The Object Is Absent ran from October 19 to 27, 2019, an exhibition that, by its own description, replaced objects with designers acting, singing and dancing. Four people are named for concept, curating and realization: Alexandre Humbert, Tom Loois, Lucas Maassen and Spaninks.
It was later a nominee in the product category of the Dutch Design Awards, whose page quotes the jury calling the absence of objects perhaps necessary to generate new ways of designing.

The Self Design Academy ran from September 18 to November 22, 2020, as a joint initiative of MU and the Image Society, curated by Mieke Gerritzen and Spaninks, with 18 artists and designers, shown both at MU and online.
In December MU opened Evolutionaries for the tenth anniversary of the Bio Art & Design Award.

This year needs care. The album is titled Bio.Stories, but MU's archive has no exhibition by that name. MU's show that October was LAWKI-Alive, by the collective ARK, from October 14 to November 28, 2021, curated by Spaninks and Paulien Dresscher.

Bio.Stories was a separate event hosted in MU: a forum series curated by the design consultancy Faber Futures with the World Economic Forum's Global Future Council on Synthetic Biology, which a participant announced for MU at Torenallee 40-06 on October 19, 2021.
So the 141 photographs titled Bio.Stories document a forum held in MU's hall, and the album title is accurate about what it shows.

The album has 245 photographs, the largest, and titles that name no show. MU's archive supplies one. Reproduction Otherwise, on view from October 7 to November 27, 2022, looked at designers' and artists' scenarios for human reproduction through seven makers.

The Creative Industries Fund NL was also in MU that week, with a video installation of one-minute portraits of 51 talents and a live program, and its own report credits photographs of it to Max Kneefel, the photographer named across the MU album.

I connect the album to Reproduction Otherwise by date, since it was the MU exhibition on show on October 22, 2022, and not by any title. As an anatomist, I know reproduction as a chapter of structure and function. MU's exhibition text treats it as a set of social, religious, medical and economic systems, which is a different way into the same subject, and I take no position on its argument here.

I found no 2023 album, and I cannot say whether one exists. What I can say is that MU was open with a show during DDW 2023: TIMELESSTIME by MAISON the FAUX, an installation with scheduled performances, running from September 15 to November 26, 2023, with its DDW-week performances on October 21, 22 and 25 to 29, from 2 to 5 p.m.
The BAD Award exhibition followed on December 15, 2023.
Poetics of Prompting, a collaboration between The Hmm and MU, ran from October 4 to November 24, 2024. MU's page describes it as exploring new languages between AI and human creativity.
DDW's press page, read on October 6, names it as MU's show for that DDW.

Other Intelligences ran from October 10 to November 23, 2025, curated by Sabine Himmelsbach, Marlene Wenger and Spaninks. MU's page says twelve artists took part but prints thirteen names, and I cannot tell which count is right.
The album's titles name works including Plant Machete by David Bowen and PL_AI by Špela Petrič.
MU's 2017 to 2020 plan had already listed Petrič among the artists MU was in conversation with.

blocks.x: Beyond the main show, and who pays

r: The archive also lists smaller DDW-week items that the photo albums fold into one title. A daily design talk show called Create Out Loud appears in the archive on October 18, 2015, October 21, 2016, October 22, 2017 and October 21, 2018.

MU's activity plan says MU set it up with the Design Academy Eindhoven, the Creative Industries Fund NL and Dutch Design Week, and that it wanted a daily moment of reflection on design that the festival lacked.

Other DDW-week entries include Dries Verhoeven's Guilty Landscapes IV in 2016, Embassy of Intimacy in 2017 and The Scene Is Here in 2019, each listed with a start date and nothing more in the list view.
The albums cannot tell a reader which of these a photograph belongs to.

MU's money is public and mixed. Its organization page says it is structurally supported by the Ministry of OCW, the province of North Brabant and the Cultuur Eindhoven foundation with the municipality, and that it receives project support from funds including Fonds21, Kunstloc Brabant, the Creative Industries Fund NL, the VSB Fonds and the Cultural Participation Fund.

The 2017 to 2020 plan describes a three-part model of income from its own activities, sponsors and media, and outside funds, with public subsidy named as the most important source. It also says the staff then consisted of eight listed roles, with the director's time partly lent to the STRP biennial.
The Brabant Cultureel article adds that the national subsidy has to be requested again every four years.
I mention this because a venue that depends on fixed funding periods tends to plan in blocks, and MU's calendar reads that way.

blocks.x: Threads that run through the years

r: Three patterns show up only when the exhibition archive is read next to the photo archive.

First, the calendar. In most years MU opens its autumn show in the first half of October and keeps it up for weeks after the festival ends: October 5 to 25 in 2015, October 7 to November 13 in 2016, October 6 to November 12 in 2017, October 12 to November 11 in 2018, October 7 to November 27 in 2022, October 4 to November 24 in 2024 and October 10 to November 23 in 2025. 2019 is the exception, with The Object Is Absent running only from October 19 to 27. For 2026, MU's press page gives the opening as October 9 and the exhibition page as October 10.

The activity plan explains one reason for the long runs. It says each changeover closes the space to the public for at least two weeks and that MU therefore planned no more than six presentations a year in its own space.
Second, the director's hand. Spaninks is named as curator or co-curator of the DDW-season show in 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2025 and 2026.
In 2016 the co-curators were Muiser and Loois.
That is a pattern of a standing house curator working with a changing guest, and I take it from the credits and not from any statement by MU.
Third, return visits. Joey Holder is in the 2017 and 2025 exhibitions.
MAISON the FAUX made TIMELESSTIME in 2023 and returns in 2026 with Everything Moist Seems Alive.
The bio artist behind this year's Bar Mycelium, Dasha Tsapenko, was one of the three winners of the 2020 Bio Art & Design Award.
MU says on its About page that the award is on hold for now while it looks for partners and funds.

blocks.x: What MU lists for DDW 2026

r: DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and MU's own page for it lists six items.

The main one is Everything Moist Seems Alive by MAISON the FAUX, which MU's page calls an installation and string of live performances that drips, flows, splashes, seeps, leaks and sweats. It is a co-production of the foundation This is not an Office, MU and Studio Boekman, and it runs to January 3, 2027, with live performances daily in DDW week except October 19 and 20.
Bar Mycelium is in the MU container at Plug-In City, a bar grown from mycelium with a mycologist and a biotechnologist, with free admission to the bar and booked slots for cocktail sessions.

The page also lists Small & Slow AI by the Visual Methodologies Collective, an AI workshop program from The Hmm for ages 8 and up, a presentation by the Creative Industries Fund NL and a pop-up bookshop by Motta Art Books.
I describe these only as MU lists them.

One more item concerns the organization more than the program. A report on the local news site eindhoven.nieuws.nl says the art and technology festival STRP will stop at the end of 2026, and that its digital archive and website will go to MU.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I cannot say whether Gerard is the former SAN, built in 1929, or the former SBP, built in 1930. RVO and a French database disagree, and the register entry does not label the buildings. I also cannot say what Philips made on MU's particular floor, beyond the site being a radio-factory complex.
I do not have a source that explains Trudo's 2014. I have reasoned that the Strijp-S space opened in 2013 and the old home closed in 2014, but I have not seen it written in one place.
Every Flickr count and photographer credit rests on my October 6 reading, which I could not repeat. I do not know whether a 2023 album exists, or why the 2024 album has only eight photographs.
I have visitor figures only for DDW 2014 and for the 2017 to 2020 plan's general range, nothing for later years. The 2025 to 2028 multi-year plan that MU links from its site was not retrievable.

Two sites that carry coverage of these shows, Dezeen and Faber Futures, refused my requests with an access-denied answer, so I stopped asking and did not open them. Where this essay needs facts from them, it takes them from MU's own archive or from a participant's announcement.

If you want to test this record yourself, take the year you remember best, find its dates in MU's exhibition archive, and ask what that show, which usually ran for weeks, left out of the one festival week the photographs cover.

posts.title: Natlab: a physics laboratory from 1923, a cinema since 2013, and a design week that keeps asking it about research
posts.subtitle: A former Philips research building on Strijp-S, followed through heritage writing, the organizers' own archives and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Natlab Eindhoven: from physics lab to cinema
posts.description: Natlab on Strijp-S: a Philips laboratory founded in 1914, in its own building from 1923, a cinema since 2013, and a Dutch Design Week venue.

r: Natlab is older than its building: the Philips physics laboratory began in 1914 inside a lamp factory and moved into the Kastanjelaan building in 1923.

Two founding dates are in circulation for the NatLab, and they describe different things; the sources below explain how. I use public sources only: heritage writing from the Eindhoven architecture center, a 2002 book review in a Dutch academic magazine, the municipality's and the architects' own descriptions of the conversion, the archives of the lab Baltan, which works inside the building, the Dutch Design Week (DDW) program listings and the official DDW photo archive on Flickr. This essay reports no visit and no interview.

I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was for before I ask what it is now. A research building that now holds a cinema, a school, a lab for artists and a professionals' conference is a fair test of that habit.

blocks.x: The laboratory began in a lamp factory in 1914

r: The historian Klaas van Berkel, reviewing a dissertation on the lab in 2002, says the NatLab officially begins in 1914, when Gilles Holst came to Eindhoven as its first director, and calls that a fairly arbitrary starting date.

Gerard Philips was already doing chemical experiments in the factory in the 1890s. In 1908 he hired a chemical engineer, J.C. Lokker, who got a small laboratory on the fifth floor that the staff called the little pharmacy. In 1913 a second engineer, L. Hamburger, arrived and became the first Philips researcher to do fundamental scientific work. Van Berkel adds that Dutch patent law, in force since 1912, gave companies a reason to do their own research.
Holst's group got space on the fourth floor, and staff called the chemists' lab Lab V and the physicists' lab Lab IV.

A TU/e page agrees on the date and the motive. It says the NatLab was founded in 1914 after a direct decision by Gerard and Anton Philips, who wanted in-house research to support product development, a patent portfolio and less reliance on other firms' patents.

The separate building came later. Van Berkel says the lab outgrew the factory floors and was housed in its own laboratory in Strijp, then at the edge of Eindhoven, so that in 1923, almost ten years after Holst arrived, "the actual NatLab" was born.

The Eindhoven architecture center, Architectuurcentrum Eindhoven, gives the same year and adds the details. The lab had been housed in the Philips complex on the Emmasingel. In 1923 it got its own building on Strijp-S, designed by the architect Dirk Roosenburg, with the Philips building code SMM.
The same article says there were 15 researchers and 20 assistants in 1923 and 106 researchers and 360 assistants by 1939.

So the two dates are both right. 1914 is the laboratory, and 1923 is this building. A plaque with the words Natuurkundig Laboratorium 1923 is among the details the architecture center lists in the building.
It would therefore be wrong to say that Philips opened the laboratory here in 1923. Philips moved an existing laboratory into this building in 1923.

blocks.x: What happened inside it

r: The architecture center's article says Albert Einstein visited in 1923 and caused a stir in Eindhoven. It says short-wave radio broadcasts to the Dutch East Indies started from the NatLab, and that in 1927 Queen Wilhelmina and Princess Juliana addressed the colony from the building, which is why one room is still called the Queen's Room.
The Strijp-S site's own history page confirms the Queen's radio address from the laboratory.

Television came next. The article says an annex of the NatLab served as a television studio from 1946, and that between 1948 and 1951 Philips made 264 experimental broadcasts with transmitters on the top floor of the Veemgebouw, another Strijp-S building, topped by a wooden mast.
The article calls them experimental broadcasts, and I do not claim more than that.

Then there is sound. A 2010 text from the VPRO radio archive by the journalist Marten Minkema, now hosted on a site about the lab's history, says the composers Tom Dissevelt and Dick Raaijmakers were given modern equipment in an acoustics department between 1956 and 1960 to experiment with electronic sound, which produced the piece Song of the Second Moon and puzzlement elsewhere in Philips.
Strijp-S's history page says Philips saw nothing in the project and put no more energy into it.
The architecture center explains where the name Baltan comes from. Raaijmakers recorded as Kid Baltan, which is Natlab and Dik read backwards.

The lab was also a social place. A mural by the artist Albert Troost, in the auditorium, was presented on December 21, 1957 by the 1,300 staff then working at the NatLab, at the opening of a new wing and the 40th anniversary of Philips Research.

The mural's own contents, as the architecture center quotes the local newspaper's 1957 description, show an inventor handing a crystal on until humanity benefits, and a falling figure surrounded by fire for the misuse of inventions.

After the war, Minkema writes, the lab grew under its director Hendrik Casimir and gained a function above the company's, with more room for basic research that had nothing to do with shavers or irons. In the mid-1970s it cost 250 million guilders a year and employed 2,000 people, and a 1990 cost-cutting operation ended its special position inside the group.
The architecture center says the NatLab moved to Waalre in 1963 and that the campus, opened to other companies in 2003, is now the High Tech Campus.
The TU/e page says the move happened in the early 1960s, which matches.

blocks.x: How a research building became a cinema

r: The building is a municipal monument. Strijp-S's history page says so, and so does the architecture firm that converted it.

N Architecten of Maastricht, working for the municipality of Eindhoven, gives 2011 to 2014 as the design and realization period for what it calls Natlab 2.0, a re-use as a cultural center. It says the hardest task was placing a 200-seat hall in the existing building, which the firm solved with a visibly different element in weathering steel that rises above the roof line and is visible through the old windows. The café-restaurant went into the former boiler house.
The architecture center adds that the floors of the halls, the window frames and Troost's mural were kept.
The film theater Natlab opened officially on October 11, 2013, with five screens, a multipurpose stage hall, two exhibition spaces and a café-restaurant.
The tenants named in the article include the film theater Plaza Futura, the film platform Broet, Baltan, Architectuurcentrum Eindhoven and the school SintLucas.
Another part of the old complex became a SintLucas building in 2016, designed by Cepezed and Arup with Laride, and was nominated in 2017 for the municipal architecture prize named after Roosenburg.
In October 2017 the European Physical Society gave the building its Historical Site distinction. The EPS list includes The Philips NatLab, Eindhoven (2017).

The architecture center says the plaque hangs at the entrance and calls it Historical Site number 36. A TU/e page says the distinction came on October 5, 2017 and was the second given to an industrial research lab.
The plaque is therefore at the entrance of the building that is now the film theater.

blocks.x: A lab inside the lab

r: Baltan Laboratories is the organization most tied to the archive years below. Its About page says it was founded as a two-year pilot to explore what the media lab of the future could look like, and ties its identity to the NatLab and to Strijp-S, which it calls the former forbidden city. It says the renovated Natlab building opened officially with Baltan as a key inhabitant, with openings celebrated by projects inspired by Raaijmakers.
The Mediamatic listing for a 2009 session of a monthly series called BALTAN goes NATLAB puts Baltan's presentations in the auditorium of the former Philips NatLab already in May 2009.
Baltan's 2015 annual report says its offices and lab spaces in the building, which looked generous when it moved in during 2013, had become too small at full occupancy by the end of 2015.
The 2016 report says it then took office space elsewhere on Strijp-S, at the Apparatenfabriek owned by Trudo, though the lab's events kept using the Natlab address.

blocks.x: What the archive shows, year by year

r: The official DDW photo archive holds Natlab albums for 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2021 and 2025. I could not reopen Flickr for this pass, so every album count and photographer credit below stays second-hand from my October 6 reading. What I could do is find, for each year, the organizer's own account of what was on.

Baltan and the aid organization Hivos began Age of Wonderland that year. Baltan's page for an Open Social Innovation Lab on October 2 to 4, 2014 says it was a chance to work with the six international artists of the Age of Wonderland program.
The archive's tag for Natlab contains eight photographs from that year, outside the range of the albums.

The second Age of Wonderland took the theme Balancing Green and Fair Food. The Creative Industries Fund NL, which granted 40,000 euros, describes a platform and incubator program with the curator Arne Hendriks, six designers from Kyrgyzstan, Indonesia, Tanzania and Bolivia, and a six-week residency, with results shown at DDW 2015.
Baltan's annual report mentions a well-attended Future Food Seminar in Natlab and a fellow from Bishkek who researched the traditional feast Toi, which often has more than 800 guests.

The third edition was Big Data. Big DADA? Hivos says six creatives from Africa, Asia and Latin America would research big and open data and show their work at DDW, October 22 to 30, in an exhibition and workshops, with Natlab as their temporary studio from September 26 and a seminar called The Big Data/Dada Dialogues.

Baltan's report adds a pop-up radio station in Natlab during DDW and a traffic-counting system that collected real-time data on visitors to the building, a first step in a Tanzanian fellow's work to map his home city.
The two sources disagree on the fellows' home countries. Hivos names fellows from Guatemala, Indonesia and Tanzania, and the Baltan report names Indonesia, Chile, Tanzania and Iran.
The album has 62 photographs, of which I could reach 24.

The final edition was 100 Days of Learning. Baltan's year-end note says teachers from all over the world answered the question of what we need to learn to make the world better, in workshops and an exhibition, and that the exhibition would travel to another show in January.

Baltan's Frankenstein Exhibition, titled It's Alive, ran from October 20 to 28, 2018, daily from 11:00 to 18:00, on whether AI and robotics will decide for us, with us or against us. Its works include a mirror room by We Are Data, a robotic lifeform called Cluster by Quintus Glerum, a digital persona by Arthur Elsenaar and an AI training center by Bureau Moeilijke Dingen.
A Frankenstein Symposium on October 22 ran from 11:00 to 20:30 at Natlab, organized by Baltan and Robot Love, with a regular ticket price of 50 euros.

The program was Homo Sensorium, October 19 to 27, 2019. Baltan's page lists experiments, workshops, talks, dinners, tours, films and a Brainwave Wedding Lab, in which EEG sensors measure the brain activity of couples during a kiss.
I cannot say which activity the album's clear dome belongs to, and the page does not mention a dome.
That uncertainty from my earlier reading stays. The page does settle the name of the 2019 program.
No Natlab album exists in the archive for 2020, and I did not find a Baltan program for that year.

Mediamatic of Amsterdam and Baltan hosted Inhuman Carnaval at Natlab from October 17 to 22, 2021, with an open costume lab, exhibitions, workshops and talks on species from earthworms to fungi. Nearly 70 names and organizations are listed for it.
The album has nine photographs dated October 21.

No Natlab album exists for these years. The sources show where Baltan went. In 2023 it and Onomatopee presented the DDW Gym at Sectie-C, and a selection of the project moved to Baltan's exhibition space in Natlab from November 8, 2023 to January 7, 2024.
In 2024 its Decentralized Futures exhibition on blockchain and digital art was hosted at Koelhuis District Eindhoven.
Natlab itself was still in use for DDW in 2024. A CLICKNL notice says the public design program PONT held three sessions at Natlab, part of the DDW Mission Days.
Mission Days is a DDW program of curated sessions for professionals around the festival's five guiding missions.

TU Delft's page for DDW 2025 lists Design United Dialogue sessions at Natlab from 9:30 to 12:30 on October 20, for Living Environment, and October 21, for Thriving Planet, and says sessions continued through October 24 with registration.
The album has 112 photographs of what its titles call Mission Days, with a stage and round tables in the first ones I viewed.
That is a conference, and it is a different use of the building from any earlier year.

blocks.x: Who paid for the research on view

r: Baltan's own reports show how thin the funding behind these shows could be. The 2015 report says a small team of three permanent staff, plus freelancers, interns and volunteers, produced that year's work, and that Baltan worked structurally with the Holst Centre, an open innovation technology center.

The 2016 report is blunter. It says an application to the Creative Industries Fund NL for basic infrastructure was rejected, that Age of Wonderland had to pull out all stops after refusals from the fund and from Brabant C, and that Baltan responded by creating a partner program, MEET : IMPACT, whose first partner event took place in October during DDW and Age of Wonderland.
The December 2017 note says the Creative Industries Fund NL granted Baltan's program for the following year, with continued partnership with the Holst Centre and Sensiks.
Research on public view in this building was, in other words, financed project by project.

blocks.x: A reading of the sequence

r: Read in order, the years describe a building that first showed research to the public and later hosted professionals who talk about it.

From 2014 to 2021 the organizer's own accounts describe residencies, exhibitions, a radio station, a symposium and a costume lab, all of them open to visitors. From 2024 on, the sources describe sessions for professionals, some of them with registration. The 2026 listing fits that pattern.
The DDW 2026 location page gives Natlab weekday hours of 9:30 to 13:30 from October 19 to 23 and shows the building closed on October 17, 18, 24 and 25.

The four items it shows at the time of reading are a regional care seminar by the Catharina Hospital on October 22, the Design United Dialogues from October 19 to 23, a workshop called Repositioning Circularity on October 20 and a Netherlands China Design Symposium on October 19.
The page may list more, because it offers a link to all program items.

That is my reading, and the evidence for it is uneven. Baltan's DDW shows were held elsewhere in 2023 and 2024, which fits the pattern, and a single Mission Days album does not prove a trend. The Baltan expo space in Natlab was still showing projects in November 2023.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: The building history here rests on the architecture center's article, a book review and a radio feature, which cite an unpublished 2008 building-history report by Suzanne Fischer and a book on the lab that I did not read. I did not find an open primary document for the Einstein visit or the 1927 radio address. The Strijp-S history page confirms the radio address only.

Two places that would help did not answer: the cinema's own site returned a server error to my robots.txt request, and an Italian web magazine that covered Baltan returned an access-denied answer, so I stopped asking and used neither.

I do not know why there is no album for 2020 or 2022, what happened at Natlab in DDW 2022, which activity the 2019 dome belonged to, or how many people visited in any year. Baltan's reports give some counts for its own events, and none for DDW weeks. The Flickr counts and credits come from my October 6 reading.

One more thing remains unclear. Baltan's About page dates the official opening of the renovated building to its 2014 to 2015 period, while the architecture center says October 11, 2013, and the architects give 2011 to 2014 for design and realization. I take the architecture center's date for the film theater's opening, and the other dates may describe other parts of the work.

If you go during DDW 2026, check the hours first. Then look for the plaque by the entrance, and ask which of the two stories on the 1957 mural still describes this building: the crystal passed from hand to hand until humanity benefits, or the figure falling through fire.

posts.title: The NRE terrein: a gasworks from 1899, a bombed gas holder and a neighborhood built by the people who use it
posts.subtitle: A former municipal energy site in Eindhoven, followed through heritage writing, the planners' and architects' own accounts and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
posts.seoTitle: NRE terrein Eindhoven: gasworks to design site
posts.description: The NRE terrein in Eindhoven, from an 1899 gasworks to a creative neighborhood and Dutch Design Week venue, with what the sources do and do not show.

r: The NRE terrein in Eindhoven began as a gasworks in 1899 and was rebuilt in the 2010s by its future users, without a project developer.

The dates for this site conflict across the sources, so I say below which source supports which year. This essay uses public sources only: the provincial heritage body Erfgoed Brabant, the architects and planners who worked on the site, the collective NUL ZES, the city's tourism pages, Dutch Design Week (DDW) location pages and the official DDW photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview. A few pages I wanted refused automated requests, and I name them at the end.

I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was for before I ask what it is now. A gasworks, a power station and a set of workshops for the city's utilities are a good place to practice it, because each of them kept the city's lights and stoves running and none was built to be looked at.

blocks.x: A gasworks moved to the canal in 1899

r: Erfgoed Brabant Verhalen, the heritage body's story site, dates the start of the site to 1899, when Eindhoven's first gasworks was moved out of the inner city to a spot on the Eindhovens Kanaal. The canal meant the city's residents would suffer less from the plant, and coal could be unloaded straight from the water. The building was designed by Louis Kooken, the city architect, and some years later large gas holders were added to store gas.

In 1909 the company Maatschappij de Peelcentrale began building an electricity plant on the site, finished in 1912, and in 1924 the site gained the Zuiverhuis, a purification house where gas was cleaned with water.

The gasworks itself fell out of use as early as 1930, because technical progress allowed gas to travel farther, and the city took cheaper mine gas from the state mines. A receiving station for mine gas came instead. The water-gas plant stayed in use, the article says, because Philips still needed it.

That last sentence matters for a series about Eindhoven's technology history. Philips appears here as a customer of the water-gas plant, not as the owner, and the site remained a municipal utility site.

The firm Diederendirrix gives the setting. The Eindhovens Kanaal was dug in 1846 and made it cheap to move coal, wood and heavy machines, so factories collected at its end near the city. The wood company N.V. Picus began around 1883 and went bankrupt in 1993. Hub van Doorne started the workshop that became the truck maker DAF behind a brewery on the same stretch in 1928, and the linked buildings on the Tongelresestraat that remain now hold the DAF Museum.

The whole former industrial estate covered 6.5 hectares, held buildings from 1899 to 1992, and was kept alive by re-use and temporary use until a selection of buildings designated as monuments remained.

blocks.x: The gas holder called Goliath

r: In 1941 one of the gas holders, the 84-meter Goliath, was hit in a British bombing raid and burned out. In 1944, during the liberation, other holders were damaged. In 1953 a new office building by the Eindhoven architect Cees Geenen was added.

A local photo-history site gives more detail from the same event: it says the holder, built in 1930, was a landmark for pilots at 84 meters and burned out in the night of March 3 to 4, 1941, and that its flame lit up the whole city.

That site is a collection of photographs and reader comments, so I treat its details as local memory and not as a record. It also says the holder was demolished in 1970, after a fire during demolition work on September 29 of that year.
The heritage article says the holders were removed in the 1960s.
I could not reconcile those two, and the site's own stories do not need the answer.

In the 1960s, the heritage article continues, storage and distribution left the complex, the holders were demolished and the offices and workshops stayed. In 1989 the municipal utilities for gas, water and electricity were merged into the company NV Nutsbedrijven Regio Eindhoven, NRE, which gives the terrain its name.
The utility later moved to another location.

blocks.x: The dates line up once the sources are read together

r: Several sources give different-looking accounts of the end of the utility years, and most of the difference disappears when the urban designers' history is added. Diederendirrix, the architecture and urban design firm that wrote the first vision for the area, says the gasworks premises became part of Nutsbedrijven Regio Eindhoven, that NRE became part of the grid operator Enexis and that it left the premises in 2010. After that, it says, a number of municipal services moved into the existing office building and workplaces.
The city tourism page agrees that the utilities were on the site from 1989 to 2010 and that the municipality bought the site afterwards.

A heritage re-use site says that NRE became Endinet in 2007, that it was already clear Endinet would leave, and that the municipality bought the complex in 2010. A second page by the same site repeats the 2010 purchase.

Two dates in the record then look out of place. A 2019 municipal report written for an EU project, which I read on October 7 and could not open again because its host now refuses my requests, says the municipality acquired the site in 2004 and that Endinet left in 2012.

The 2004 has a likely source. Diederendirrix says it started in 2004 with an urban development vision for the area, so I read the 2004 in that report as the vision and not the purchase, though no page says so.
The 2012 is a single second-hand statement against several pages for 2010, and I leave it aside.
One more date needs care. Most sources date the gasworks to 1899. Diederendirrix says the coal gas factory opened in 1900 at the Havenhoofd, the head of the canal.
A start of building in 1899 and an opening in 1900 would fit both, but that reconciliation is mine.

blocks.x: Ten years of building it from the inside

r: The planners' and architects' accounts agree on an unusual method. The urban design firm Van Tuijn Stedenbouw says the terrain was long a blank spot on the map, closed to most people, and that during the planning years it was opened to temporary activities and became a creative hotspot. Its description of the process says there was no fixed master plan, that only end users and stakeholders took part, and that the area was shaped cooperatively with the new residents and businesses.

The architects Houben / Van Mierlo describe the same arc: after a period of temporary use the municipality issued buildings and building plots to private initiators, whose first generation drew up, with their advisers, the municipality and the TU/e's Bauhütte, a framework plan called Nieuwe Energie, new energy.

The planning economists Metafoor, who worked for the municipality, give dates: the development process started in 2013 with small private parties and end users, with no housing corporations or project developers; the site covers 2.1 hectares; a provincial subsidy helped pay for cleaning up the ground and replacing the sewer; and the last phase of public space was due to be delivered in 2022.

Houben / Van Mierlo add that the plan Made by NRE was selected by the municipality in early 2018 to redevelop the last four plots. It is a collective of residents, entrepreneurs, designers and makers, and it produced four buildings called Ambachtsdorp, Park NRE, Werkgebouw and Body Building. The firm says that with Made by NRE the transformation of the terrain is complete.

The monument status is disputed. The re-use site lists the former gasworks building as a municipal monument, with Louis Kooken as the original architect and De Bever architecten for the transformation.
Diederendirrix says a selection of buildings designated as monuments remained.
Van Tuijn says the existing buildings have no monumental status but do have cultural-historical value.

Two of the three say there are designated buildings, and I cannot tell from these pages which buildings or what level of designation, so the municipal monument list is the place to check. The re-use site also gives two transformation years for the same building, 2013 on one page and 2019 on the page about the jazz club that occupies it.

An undated guide from the Eindhoven-Now site lists eleven remarkable factory buildings on the terrain and, from the temporary period, the Atelierdorp with 24 studios, a bakery, a coffee bar and an exhibition space, and the events venue FIFTH|NRE waiting for its planned conversion to a jazz club.

blocks.x: NUL ZES, the collective that says it grew up here

r: NUL ZES is a collective of creative professionals at Gasfabriek 3A. Its own site says it grew up at NRE, that the old industrial buildings and all the new plots were developed by their end users with no project developer, and that NUL ZES took part as first-time placemakers, helped found the neighborhood association and developed the identity of NRE, including a logo. It offers private studios for a limited number of members, shared wood, metal and ceramics workshops, and event spaces.

For DDW 2026 its page on the festival site lists it as a free location open from 11:00 to 20:00 each day, with items that include Touch On Connection by Plura Studio and a presentation by NUL ZES members.

blocks.x: What the DDW archive shows

r: The DDW photo archive on Flickr holds albums titled NRE for 2016, 2017, 2018, 2024 and 2025, six albums and 77 photos by my October 7 count. I could not reopen Flickr for this pass, so all counts, credits and picture descriptions in this section are second-hand.

The 2016 album has 13 photos by Iris Rijskamp, showing a long table of photographs in a dark hall, a yard with a yellow van and brick sheds, and weathered halls with plinths. The 2017 album has 10 photos by Nick Bookelaar, including a white wall of small framed works, a brick workshop with ceramics and the front of the NulZes building with bicycles. The 2018 album has 13 photos by the same photographer, and its title names three sets of makers: Lotte de Raadt with Kirstie van Noort, Alissa and Nienke, and NulZes. The 2024 album has 11 photos by Anwyn Howarth, with a rooftop garden pavilion called Cooling Down the City and exhibition rooms called Lighting for Wellbeing. The two 2025 albums, Finished Forms with 26 photos and Zowa with four, are by Cleo Goossens.
There is no album titled NRE for 2015 or 2019 to 2023, though albums under maker or event names exist for several of those years.

For the festival's own account I used its 2026 location pages. Make Eindhoven, at Gasfabriek 12, offers workshops for graphic techniques, glass, metal and CAD/CAM and sits in what the page calls the former workshop of the energy companies on the NRE site. It is free and open from 11:00 to 18:00.
Fifth, at Gasfabriek 5, describes itself as set in the industrial and cultural NRE site.
Bart Hess I NRE is at Gashouder 43A, and its page calls the terrain a small-scale but lively creative area on the edge of the center with several design studios and creative agencies.
The city's Kanaalzone tip of October 1, 2026 says there are fifteen DDW projects at the NRE site.
The first year the site was used for DDW remains unknown. The 2019 municipal report says it hosted DDW and GLOW years before the buildings were sold, and names no year.

GLOW's own page for the work Waterfalls of Light says the light festival covered the facade of the three-story NRE office building at the head of the canal, built in 1992, with 40,000 small lights; the text I read gives no year.

blocks.x: A reading of the site

r: Read together, these sources describe a place whose use changed in stages that were each decided by its users: the utility that left, a period of temporary tenants who made it a hotspot, and then a set of buildings issued piece by piece to the people who had been using them.

A nine-day festival fits that pattern of temporary use, and the archive's gaps in 2019 to 2023 may say more about how the albums were titled than about what happened on site. That second point is a guess, and I cannot confirm it.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I take 2010 for both the departure of the utility and the municipal purchase, on the strength of four pages, but I did not find a deed or a council decision, and the one document that says 2004 and 2012 could not be re-opened.

I do not know when DDW first used the site, or what the 2016 album shows beyond its photographs, because I could not reopen Flickr. I do not know which buildings are designated monuments. I do not know when the large gas holder was demolished. The heritage article says the 1960s and a photo-history site says 1970.

The most detailed document I could not read is a zoning-plan explanation for the area, hosted on a viewer site that refused my request, and a European heritage hub that also refused. I stopped asking both and did not look for copies elsewhere.

If a gasworks can become a festival venue, a neighborhood and a set of private workshops within a decade, which of its records would you ask the city to keep: the plans, the temporary tenants' agreements, or the photographs?

posts.title: The Ontdekfabriek: a radio-equipment factory, a children's workshop and a move planned for the end of 2026
posts.subtitle: A hands-on making space in a former Philips building on Strijp-S, followed through the building's register entries, the foundation's own reports and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Ontdekfabriek Eindhoven: factory, workshop, move
posts.description: The Ontdekfabriek on Strijp-S: a Philips radio-equipment factory, a children's workshop since about 2010, and a move planned for the end of 2026.

r: The Ontdekfabriek has spent about sixteen years as a children's workshop on the ground floor of a former Philips radio-equipment factory on Strijp-S, and a May 2026 report says it has to leave that building at the end of this year.

That makes this a good moment to read its record. This essay uses public sources only: the foundation's own website and annual reports, the national monument register, the Strijp-S developers' pages, trade-press reports on the move and the official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview. I describe the venue's audience only as the venue describes it, and I mention no participant in any photograph.

As a medical educator, I care about how people learn by handling things, so the venue's own account of its method is the part I read most closely. I read it as a description of a teaching sequence and I take no position on how well it works.

blocks.x: The building was a radio-equipment factory

r: Strijp-S's page for the Apparatenfabriek, which means appliance factory, says it was formerly better known as building SK and was built as the first radio equipment factory. It says the first Philips radios were produced there and that after the Second World War it made television sets. Housing corporation Trudo turned it into a business center in 2013, with a national monument status noted on the page.
The same page says three buildings rose in 1928 on the Hoge Rug: Anton, Gerard and the Apparatenfabriek.

That year does not match the building historians. A survey written for the municipality of Eindhoven by the building-history firm of J.A. van der Hoeve gives SK as 1927, SAN as 1929 and SBP as 1930, and says the buildings belong to a radio factory that took over most of the site from the mid-1920s.

The national monument register lists the three buildings as one monument, number 518771, and says they were built in 1930, 1929 and 1927 to a design by the Philips engineer A. de Broekert. Its address list for the monument includes Torenallee 22, the Ontdekfabriek's address.
Philips's own media library says the company introduced its first radio in 1927, built entirely from Philips components.
I take 1927 for SK, because two documents that rest on the buildings themselves agree, and treat Strijp-S's 1928 as a round year for the row.

The developers describe what came after. Driehoek Strijp-S says the Apparatenfabriek was still in Philips use until shortly before its transformation, that the ground floor and first floor were rebuilt for public functions, and that the ground floor housed the Ontdekfabriek, Capital D, Yksi, the 5Minuten Museum and Caffee Allee.

blocks.x: Founded in 2009, open from about 2010

r: Three sources give three founding years, and they turn out to be counting different things. The foundation's own ANBI page, the Dutch tax status for charities, says Stichting De Ontdekfabriek was established on May 18, 2009.

A 2020 article on the Driehoek Strijp-S site, published on February 11 to mark ten years of the venue, says it started in the building that now holds the Urban Shopper, with very few facilities, and was open only on Sundays at first, under Anne Veenstra, who had run Plan-2 in the Klokgebouw.
A 2017 article by E52 in the IO+ archive quotes the co-founder Chris Voets saying he started the venue with Hugo Vrijdag seven years earlier, which points to 2010.

So the foundation dates from 2009 and the public venue from about 2010. The first reading is a legal date and the second is an opening date, and I say that on my own reasoning. The foundation's 2024 report is consistent with 2009, since it carries a caption about celebrating its 15th anniversary.

The 2020 article adds three facts. At the ten-year party Trudo handed over the brand name De Ontdekfabriek, which it had owned. The venue had already expanded to Breda under the name De Uitvindfabriek. And the location in the Apparatenfabriek was uncertain from the start, because the building was at one point to be demolished, until a decision that it would stay for at least five more years.
A national monument and a demolition plan sit oddly together, and I cannot explain it from these pages.

blocks.x: How the venue describes its own method

r: Chris Voets, quoted in the 2020 article, says three quarters of the visitors are parents with children who come to play without a reservation, and that the venue is fun from about age five or six. He describes a sequence: first a film room for inspiration, then a workshop to make something, then a presentation of the result with tools that include a film studio. He says the basic concept is ten years old, that the venue is hands-on and uses few digital tools, and that it aims to teach the creative step that comes before programming.
The E52 article records the same idea in his words: a child should get a first spark, and the point is doing and making, not education as such.

The foundation's statutes, as its site quotes them, set the mission as stimulating a positive attitude toward innovation, technology, science and creativity in children, with a sustainable society as a source of inspiration, by running a play-workshop and hands-on museum and offering cultural education programs.
The site describes a storytelling approach in which children and young people are inspired to investigate, design, build and present in their own way.

On ages, the venue's own pages disagree with each other. Its profile page says 4 to 18. Its practical-information page gives an indication of 4 to 12 for a family adventure. Its 2025 to 2028 policy plan says 7 to 15.
Voets's remark about age five or six is a fourth figure. I print no single range.

blocks.x: What the reports count

r: The policy plan for 2025 to 2028 says the foundation, established in 2009, reaches 30,000 children and young people a year, half through school and half in their free time with parents, and that it is a regional institution that works with Brainport, the culture-education center CultuurStation, the Dutch Design Foundation, the light festival GLOW and its sister institutions in Breda and Utrecht.

The 2025 report gives a table. It counts 231 public openings with a reach of 21,322, against a planned 165 with 21,875, and 249 school-bound activities with a reach of 13,734. Together with company events, the venue's physical reach was 21,957 in 250 offerings. The report says the foundation was open nine more days than the year before, that school visits from the city of Eindhoven rose from 37 to 50 percent of primary-school visits, that it organized 33 events, and that a children's light project for GLOW reached an estimated 15,000 children, a number kept out of the venue's visitor figures. It also reports a record turnover of just over 1.2 million euros and a surplus of 22,000 euros, which it put into a reserve in anticipation of extra work and relocation and housing costs in 2026 and after.
The report for 2024 calls that a record year for the number of activities, and says competition from a free ASML program for primary schools lowered school visits from that sector.
The numbers are the foundation's own and have not been audited by me.

blocks.x: Work outside the building

r: The 2025 report shows how much of the work already happens elsewhere. The foundation says educational activities increasingly take place at school locations, reached by an electric bus, an electric cargo bike and bicycles with trailers, and that the number of pupils it served externally, in primary and secondary schools, rose by 82.5 percent. It gives a reason that bears on the building: visits from secondary and vocational schools to Torenallee 22 fell by 64 percent, and the report says these schools often want to serve very large groups at once, which touches the limits of what the foundation can offer well given its space, machines and materials.

Among the 33 events it ran, the report names projector building at the Philips Stadion for a school challenge, car building at a discovery festival, and the final of a project called Jouw Eindhoven van de Toekomst in the Eindhoven city hall.

It also reports that a program for young people aged 14 to 18 stalled in 2025 and that it applied with the Association of Science Centers for funding from ASML to restart work with that age group in 2026.
That fits the plan's emphasis on a renovated space with a place for young people in their free time.

blocks.x: What the DDW archive shows

r: The DDW photo archive on Flickr holds Ontdekfabriek albums for 2015, 2016, 2017 and 2018, four albums with 56 photos in all by my October 7 count, and none after 2018. I could not reopen Flickr for this pass, so every count, credit and description in this section is second-hand.

The 2015 album has 20 photos by Boudewijn Bollmann, the 2016 album 13 by Nick Bookelaar, and the 2017 and 2018 albums 11 and 12 by Max Kneefel. The pictures I viewed then show workbenches with drill presses, pendant lamps, a green-screen room, a container workshop at the entrance, a gear wall and soldering and laser-cutting benches. They show the equipment and the rooms and I say nothing about the visitors.

I found no organizer's account of what the venue did for DDW in those four years, and the foundation's reports for 2024 and 2025 do not mention DDW by name. The 2025 to 2028 plan names the Dutch Design Foundation, which organizes DDW, among its cultural partners.

On the festival's 2026 location list, which I read on October 9, the Ontdekfabriek does not appear. Other organizations are listed at the same building: Community Square and Foundation We Are at Torenallee 22-04 and New Order of Fashion LAB at Torenallee 22-06.
The list may not be complete, and I cannot say why the archive stops after 2018.

blocks.x: The move

r: The policy plan describes an Ontdekfabriek 2.0: a trilogy of new adventures, a renovated space, a creative breeding ground for young people and a rehousing that is necessary because the building the foundation occupies is to be renovated, planned with the owner Trudo and the area developer Park Strijp Beheer.

The 2025 report says a permit has been applied for to build the 2.0 location in the Evoluonpark, on the Toekomst Campus, that there are agreements for an option to buy this circular building, that the province of North Brabant intends to lend part of the purchase price, and that the foundation is looking for more funding, including from the municipality.

Architecture trade press says what the building is. The Natural Pavilion, a nearly fully bio-based and demountable pavilion designed by DP6 for the Dutch government at the Floriade Expo 2022 in Almere, is to be moved to the park behind the Evoluon, on the spot where the Smartest Home of the Netherlands once stood, as the new home of the Ontdekfabriek. Because of a renovation the foundation must leave its current location in the Apparatenfabriek at the end of the year, and the ambition is to bring the building into use at the end of 2026.
Het Houtblad, a timber trade magazine, gives the same ambition and adds that the son of the Evoluon's architect Leo de Bever is advising on its position in the park.

So the 2026 edition of Dutch Design Week may be the last one that falls while the foundation is still at Torenallee 22. That is my inference from the move dates in the reports, and I have no source that says the foundation will or will not take part this year.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know what the Ontdekfabriek did at DDW in 2015 to 2018, why the archive stops after 2018, or whether it takes part in 2026. I do not know when the move will actually happen, because the end of 2026 is an ambition stated in trade-press reports and I found no later confirmation.

I do not know which age range to print, because the foundation itself gives three. I cannot explain why a national monument was once expected to be demolished. And I could not reopen Flickr, so the albums remain a second-hand record.

If you pass Torenallee 22 in DDW week, ask what a radio-equipment factory, a children's workshop and a pavilion rebuilt for its third life have in common, and which of the three you would keep a record of.
