posts.title: Sectie-C: a switchboard factory, a creative district, and a city purchase in progress
posts.subtitle: A former factory complex in Eindhoven's Tongelre district, followed through municipal documents, the owners' pages, local press and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Sectie-C Eindhoven: factory to creative district
posts.description: Sectie-C in Eindhoven, from a Philips-built complex and a Nolte and Stork factory to a Dutch Design Week venue and a planned city purchase.

r: By the accounts I could find, parts of Sectie-C were built for Philips, the complex became an electrical factory in 1970, it stood empty after 2007, designers moved in from 2010, and in March 2026 the city of Eindhoven decided in principle to buy it.

It is easy to file Sectie-C with the Philips sites of Eindhoven, and just as easy to file it with the Stork factories of Hengelo. The record supports a little of each label and all of neither, so this essay follows the place through the documents that name it. I use public sources only: the city's area framework, the developer's pages, the tenants' own site, local and trade press, a design magazine and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive on Flickr. This essay reports no visit and no interview. Dutch Design Week 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and I describe what the published pages say about it without claiming to have seen any of it.

I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was built to do before asking what it does now. A hall that made switchboards and traffic signs, then held a swimming pool in a shipping container, is a good test of that habit.

blocks.x: The name is a land-registry term, and the neighbor is a landmark

r: A local history column in Groot Eindhoven says Sectie-C is a cadastral name for the terrain, meaning it comes from the land registry rather than from a company or a designer.

The site lies in Tongelre, on the east side of the city. The city's area framework, adopted in November 2024, describes it as bounded by the Eindhoven to Venlo railway line, the TenneT high-voltage station, Urkhovenseweg and Daalakkersweg, next to the green of the Zeggen, about ten minutes by bike from the center.

Next door is 't Karregat, which matters more to the story than a neighbor usually does. The framework says the neighborhood center was completed in 1973, designed by Frank van Klingeren (1919 to 1999), and originally put two primary schools, a library, a neighborhood center, a supermarket and a café under one roof. It sits in Herzenbroeken, a district built between 1968 and 1973 as a deliberate experiment in letting residents shape their surroundings. The city gives 't Karregat cultural-historical status and treats Sectie-C as a possible second heart for Tongelre.

The tenants have taken up the connection themselves. Sectie-C's own pages list an outdoor film screening about 't Karregat on October 11, 2024, and an evening on December 9, 2024 on Van Klingeren's ideas and what Sectie-C might learn from them.

The sources do not agree on how big the place is, and the disagreement runs inside the city's own documents. NICE Developers calls it a former factory site of 6 hectares. The Open Eindhoven page puts the plan area at almost 8 hectares, and a trade-press report in March 2026 repeats "almost 8." The area framework itself says the total area is 11.3 hectares.
No source says what each figure includes, and I have not seen the boundary map that would show it, so I give none as the size of the place.
The address varies too. Dutch Design Week gives Daalakkersweg 2-14, This is Eindhoven's area tip gives 2-16, and the developer's plan site gives Daalakkersweg 2.

blocks.x: Built for Philips, taken over by Nolte in 1970

r: The oldest layer of the story comes from one source. A local history column published in Groot Eindhoven on October 5, 2024 says parts of the complex were built for the Installatie en Service Bureau of Philips. It says that in 1970 the firm Nolte Elektrotechnische en Mechanische Industrie, until then at Tongelresestraat 209, took the complex over, settled there and expanded it, making switchboards, lampposts and traffic signs.

The city's own framework points the same way without using the word Philips for the site itself: it asks for landmarks that keep alive the memory of Stork Nolte and the related industry around Philips.
No other source I opened mentions the Philips service bureau, so I treat that part as one local historian's account that I could not confirm.

Dating the buildings is harder than naming the owner. Open Eindhoven says the buildings were put up in the 1970s and 1980s. An undated student presentation hosted on a Dutch teaching platform says the buildings date from around 1970.

Those two statements fit a complex that grew in stages after Nolte arrived, which is also what the local column says Nolte did. They do not fit buildings that all predate 1970, and none of these sources dates an individual hall.

blocks.x: Stork, a spelling problem and a closing in 2007

r: The step from Nolte to Stork has a contemporary record. On June 14, 1989 the Reformatorisch Dagblad reported that Nolte Groep BV of Eindhoven would almost certainly be taken over by Verenigde Machinefabrieken Stork NV. The report gives Nolte a turnover of about 225 million guilders and about 1,900 employees, says the talks had been going for about five weeks, and quotes a board member saying it would still take a few months. Nolte was to operate inside Stork as a separate group in industrial services.
The report is about the company and says nothing about the Daalakkersweg site.
After that the chain is thinner. The Groot Eindhoven column says Nolte became Stork-Nolte and was then taken over by Strukton, and that production at the site stopped in 2007.
A trade-press report in February 2025 says Stork Nolte, "later VDL," made switchboards, lampposts and traffic signs there until 2007.
These two accounts name different later owners. I opened VDL's group history page and found no mention of Stork or Nolte, so it settles nothing.
Both agree on 2007, and the city's framework independently dates the closing of the Stork Nolte factory to 2007.
Even the company's full name wobbles. NICE Developers writes Stork-Nolte Elektrotechnische en Mechanische Industrie, and the city's framework writes "Elektronische" in the same place.
The 1989 report calls Nolte an electrotechnical company and says its electrotechnical and electronic activities would fit Stork's, so both words have a footing.
I use "electrotechnical," following the developer and the newspaper, and I cannot say which form the company registered.

blocks.x: Empty after 2007, occupied from 2010

r: The city's framework gives the shortest account of what came next: from 2010 new entrepreneurs settled on the old industrial site, and a handful of young artists and designers took over the property that had been left behind, drawn by how much could be made of the empty spaces. The framework says the name of the place became Sectie-C.
The tenants' own site agrees on 2010 as the start of the development into a creative ecosystem.
The Groot Eindhoven column says a designers' collective saw the possibilities in 2010.

The most vivid account is an interview on the developer's news site with Niels Hoebers, a stop-motion animator and artist whose studio has been at Sectie-C for 16 years. He says his group had been in a hall on Heezerweg, had to leave, and saw possibilities in what he calls the forgotten area, the former Stork Nolte location. He describes it as a playground for adults and says the group began as a collective, Collaboration O.

That is one tenant's recollection in an interview published by the developer, so I treat it as testimony and not as a settled history. It fits the 2015 description from Core77, which called Collaboration O a shared studio space housing over a dozen young designers.

blocks.x: Design Week: 2011 or 2012?

r: This is Eindhoven says Sectie-C's Dutch Design Week role started in 2011 as an accidental counterpart of the Design Week at Strijp-S, and that it has grown to more than 25,000 visitors each year.
The Groot Eindhoven column says the tenants together became a main location in 2011 and had about 25,000 visitors "then."

A contemporary report complicates the date. On October 26, 2012 the Dutch technology site Bright called Sectie C "the new location" and the biggest surprise of that year's Design Week, where even the taxi driver had to search. The reporter places it well east of the center and describes a large gate with yellow letters, a jumble of buildings and design studios, a five-meter lamp, a swimming pool in a container and a hot tub over an open fire. Sectie C is described as a breeding ground of about 80 small businesses, with the studios of Floris Wubben and Nacho Carbonell, an exhibition by the Royal College of Art from London, free design rides from the city, and opening only after 4 p.m. so that the studios could work first.

Two readings fit both sources. Sectie-C could have had a small first presence in 2011 that the 2012 reporter did not know about, or the 2011 date may be a looser reconstruction made later. I found no 2011 program, so I cannot choose. The official photo archive does not help, because its Sectie-C albums begin in 2015.

blocks.x: What the archive and the tenants' pages show, year by year

r: The Dutch Design Week Flickr account holds Sectie-C albums for eight editions between 2015 and 2024, nine albums with 402 photos in all. I read those album pages for the earlier version of this research on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen them in this pass, so the photo counts and photographer names below carry that date.
Where I can, I set them beside what Sectie-C and the press said the same year.
The album has 49 photos, with fifteen titled 91_OXI. The photographers named in titles are Iris Rijskamp, Tommy Köhlbrugge and Boudewijn Bollmann.

Core77's report of November 16, 2015 most likely explains the title: "OXI" was a group exhibition at Club-C, curated by Justine Kontou, with designers whose studios were nearby. The photo captions name Nacho Carbonell, Tessa Koot, Victor Sonna, Sabine Marcelis with Brit van Nerven, and Sander Wassink with Luuk van den Broek. Core77 also shows Studio Plott, Fleur Hulleman's "Soft Ceramics" in a small group show called "Behind the Screens," and a group exhibition called "Change of State."

The 2016 album is the largest, with 112 photos, 19 of them titled 94_SECTIEC and some dated October 26, 2016. The 2017 album has 47, with titles dated October 25, 2017. The photographers named are Rijskamp and Köhlbrugge for 2016, and Max Kneefel and Köhlbrugge for 2017.
The tenants' own site hosts a press set labeled DDW 2017.
The album has 31 photos, all credited in their titles to Max Kneefel and dated October 20, 23 and 28, 2018.

The album has 25 photos. Sectie-C's own page lists 18 items for October 19 to 27, 2019, including an exhibition on the Swiss watch brand Enicar, a project by Florian de Visser called Tourist-Site-Seeing with a Hidden Gem Shop, Wikkelhouse, and a rug collection by Studio Daniel Costa.
The archive's album is titled Oost-C, not Sectie-C, and holds 10 photos by Kneefel.

The tenants' site resolves the name. For October 17 to 25, 2020 it lists "Living Space," where, in its words, Oost-C presents itself in the large hall of Carte Blanche on Sectie-C. Studio Speciaal, described as the only design studio within Oost-C, curated it, with work by Gijs van Bon, Tijs Rooijakkers and Frits Achten, and the arrangement of objects changed through the week. The page also lists "Papercut," shown in a virtual exhibition space, from October 17 to December 31, 2020.
So Oost-C is a name used on the site for a group exhibiting inside Sectie-C. I could not check whether the 10 archive photos show this exhibition.
There are two albums, VANTOT with 35 photos and a general one with 13.

The tenants' page for "Press Play: Dutch Design Week" gives October 16 to 24, 2021, with opening hours of 11:00 to 20:00 until October 23 and 11:00 to 18:00 on October 24. It describes Sectie-C as studios of more than 100 designers, artists and photographers and as a main location with more than 25,000 visitors a year.
The 2022 album has 86 photos credited to about.today and Max Kneefel, with CollaborationO-titled photos that carry the names Fleur Hulleman and Willem van Hooff.

The titles do not say whether those two names are makers or photographers. Two other pages lean toward makers. Core77 showed a ceramics work by Fleur Hulleman at Sectie C in 2015, and Sectie-C's page lists Willem van Hooff as an exhibitor, with Olga Flor, in The Pool from May 6 to 24, 2022.

That is a lean and not a proof, because the titles themselves do not say. I found no 2023 album in the archive, although the album list I could see in the earlier pass was incomplete, and Sectie-C's list of past events has no entry dated 2023 and none for Design Week 2022.
The archive's album has only 4 photos, by Almicheal Fraay.
Sectie-C's page has a heading for Design Week 2024, October 19 to 27, titled "The Last Edition: MAYBE," with no description in the text I read.
A December 2024 exhibition called Undercurrents, hosted at Sectie-C, calls the site artist spaces that will soon undergo residential development.
The archive listing as I read it on October 7, 2026 has no Sectie-C album.

The tenants' own list for October 18 to 25, 2025 has 31 items, including a run of shows in Punt-C, several Open O studio presentations, a collaboration with 1m2 Collective, the Kunstacademie Maastricht and Rietveld alumni.

That is the clearest warning in the record. The week with the most detailed tenant listing is the week the official photo archive does not cover, so the archive shows what a photographer was sent to shoot and not how busy the site was.
Dutch Design Week lists Sectie-C open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 from October 17 to 25, 2026.

The tenants' page lists 31 items for the week. They include "A Home of Many Addresses," in which current and former residents share fifteen years of stories around the mailbox, an audio tour of listening points scanned by QR code, a project called Flavors of Sectie-C that archives the terrain's sensory memory, and a second "Radicale Wegbereiders" program with a local activity center. For neighbors, two guided tours are listed on October 17 and October 24, at 11:00 in Dutch and 15:00 in English, and a Design Week ticket is required.

blocks.x: Between the Design Weeks

r: The tenants do not wait for October. Their list shows a "Design Open" in December 2020 that joined more than ten Eindhoven designers and locations, including Piet Hein Eek, Kazerne, Kiki&Joost, Sectie-C and NRE, after the fairs they would normally show at fell away.

Later editions are listed for June 2021, December 2021, April 2022 and November 2024. The first Atelier-Sale was held on July 19, 2020 and drew on tenants who the page says number more than 250 on the former Stork-Nolte terrain.

The place also keeps small institutions of its own. The Pool is described on the site as the cultural clubhouse of Sectie-C. Anker Studio, a rehearsal and recording space, held the fourth edition of its Ankerfest on August 23, 2025.
In an interview on the developer's news site, the three founders of Anker Studio say about 150 musicians rehearse there each week, which is their figure and not an audited count.

"The Window" is a two-month artist residency on the theme of ownership. In 2025 it hosted a residency that ended with the launch of a prototype called Sectie-C Contacts on July 18, 2025, then another that ran from August 17 to October 12.

The organization behind this is two bodies. Vereniging Sectie-C represents tenants and subtenants toward the landlord, the foundation and the municipality. Stichting Sectie-C says its goal is to grow, refine and secure the creative ecosystem over the long term, and it publishes annual reports for 2023 to 2025, which I did not open.

blocks.x: 1,300 homes, a 19,500 square meter promise and a purchase in principle

r: The ownership story is the part of the record that moved most recently, and the old version of the question, who owns Sectie-C, now has an answer with a caveat. The city's framework says that since 2019 Focus on Impact has been mostly the owner, and that it owns about 90 percent of the area. It also says the municipality owns no land there beyond the public space around the plan area, so its role is facilitating.
Open Eindhoven names the owner and developer as TBFOS, short for Ten Brinke en Focus on Sectie-C.
NICE Developers says Focus acquired the complex in 2019 to safeguard its value as a breeding ground.

The planning timeline starts with the city adopting the area framework in November 2024. On February 24, 2025, Focus on Impact and Ten Brinke announced the redevelopment, with at least 1,300 homes and 30,000 square meters of business space.
A sketch design was presented to neighbors and stakeholders in April 2025, and a preliminary design was presented at two participation meetings on October 27 and November 12, 2025.

The municipality's framework sets a floor of 19,500 square meters of creative workspace. The developer's plan site repeats about 19,500 square meters of creative breeding ground, next to about 5,800 square meters of facilities, 426 student units and about 72 percent affordable housing.

The city's own page gives different figures from the developer's. It says 1,400 new homes, 85 percent affordable. The developer says 1,300 homes, about 72 percent affordable. The framework's own range is 1,100 to 1,400 homes.
I cannot tell whether these are different versions of the plan or different definitions of affordable, and I report both.

The step with the most consequence came in March 2026. A trade report of March 12, 2026 says the college of mayor and aldermen took a decision in principle to buy Sectie-C from TBFOS and to keep renting out the space, at an average rent of 85 euros per square meter of gross floor area, excluding VAT, at 2025 prices. Two other scenarios were dropped, one in which TBFOS stays owner and rents for up to 15 years and one in which the foundation becomes owner. The report gives a 50-year operating period, a first-year shortfall of about 500,000 euros and a positive result of about 600,000 euros at the end.

A second report the next day says the foundation would become main tenant and handle subletting and management, that the proposal answers a council motion of October 1, 2024 on securing creative workspace, and that 250,000 euros is set aside for the next steps. It also records that tenants are cautiously positive, worried about crowding, and unsure whether all kinds of makers can be housed, and that tenants had asked for tall spaces for mezzanines which make buildings more expensive.
Earlier, in October 2024, the tenants' association and the foundation's members had said 19,500 square meters was too little and that at least 25,000 would be needed.

This was a decision in principle. I found no source showing that the purchase has been completed, and the developer's plan page, read on October 10, 2026, presents the project as a Ten Brinke and Focus on Impact development without mentioning a municipal purchase.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: The label depends on which decade you ask about. One local historian says parts were built for Philips, the 1989 newspaper shows Stork buying Nolte, and the city says the site's industry was Stork Nolte and related industry around Philips. I give each its own era and rest the Philips claim on a single source.
Who ran the factory at the end.
Strukton (Groot Eindhoven) against VDL (PropertyNL). Not settled, and the 2007 closing date is the only point on which they agree.
6 hectares (NICE Developers), almost 8 (Open Eindhoven, repeated by Stadszaken) and 11.3 (the area framework). I could not reconcile them and use none.

Sectie-C's site says more than 250 businesses and uses "more than 100" for designers, artists and photographers in its Design Week pitch. The city's framework says about 280 tenants. This is Eindhoven's main page says over 250 artists, designers, musicians, writers and artisans and its area tip says more than 100 creatives. A 2012 report counted about 80 small businesses.

Because the city's number is from a planning document about tenants and the "more than 100" comes from promotional text about Design Week, I use about 280 for tenants and 100 only as the tenants' own Design Week claim.
Settled enough to use: the tenants' site places Oost-C inside Sectie-C in 2020.
The city and the tenants agree on 2010 for the new users. 2011 for Design Week is attributed to This is Eindhoven and a local column, but a 2012 report calls Sectie C new. Not settled.
The 25,000 figure appears on This is Eindhoven and on the tenants' 2021 page, so it is the tenants' own claim, repeated by the city's tourism site.
An undated student presentation gives about 350,000 visitors a year, which no other source supports. I did not use it.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have not found a building-by-building history. Nothing I opened dates the Philips service bureau structures, says which halls Nolte added, or says how many square meters were built when. The council's March 2026 letter is known to me only through two trade-press reports, and the council information site timed out when I tried to open a related letter, so I did not read any council document directly. A cooperation agreement between the municipality, the developer and Sectie-C is mentioned by one of those reports and I have not seen it.

I cannot say who operated the factory at the end, or whether Stork-Nolte was one business or several by 2007. I have no source for what happened to the Nolte brand name after the 1989 deal. I did not open the foundation's annual reports, and I did not re-read the Flickr albums, so every photo count and name in the year-by-year section carries its October 7 date.

I do not know why the archive has no album for 2023 or 2025, what the 10 photos of 2020 show, or whether 'Sectie C' as a land-registry term can be traced to a registry entry. I have not seen the registry itself.

If you go to Sectie-C during Dutch Design Week 2026, look at what the signs and the guided tours say about the buildings, and ask what each one is built on. When a place has had a Philips-built service complex, an electrical factory, an artists' district and a prospective city landlord, which of its names would you put on the wall?

posts.title: Stadhuisplein: a city hall that took thirty years to finish, a courthouse turned design house, and a square Design Week keeps borrowing
posts.subtitle: What municipal brochures, local press, council papers and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive show about Eindhoven's city hall, the former courthouse beside it, and the square between them
posts.seoTitle: Stadhuisplein Eindhoven: city hall, square, Design Week
posts.description: Eindhoven city hall, the former courthouse and Stadhuisplein, from a 1938 competition to Dutch Design Week 2026, with what the records do and do not show.

r: Eindhoven's city hall was the subject of a design competition in 1938, was opened by Queen Juliana on September 18, 1969, and the square in front of it was already a Dutch Design Week venue by 2009.

The official Dutch Design Week photo archive holds albums for this place in 2015, 2016 and 2025, and it is tempting to take those three years as the shape of the record. The wider sources say otherwise. The square carried a Brainport Greenhouse for the Dutch Design Awards in 2009, the building next to the city hall was a design house for years, and in 2026 the same building is a Design Week location again.

This essay follows the three places, the city hall, the former courthouse and the square, through the architecture center's heritage writing, council papers, local press and Dutch Design Week's own pages. It reports no visit and no interview. Dutch Design Week 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and I describe what its pages list without claiming to have seen any of it.

I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was built to do before asking what it is used for now. Here the building at Stadhuisplein 3 has been a court, a design house and a remembrance center within about sixty years, which makes it a good place to practice.

blocks.x: Three places that share one name

r: Stadhuisplein is the square, and the city hall stands on it. A municipal notice from January 2026 places the residents' service desk, the Inwonersplein, in the city hall at Stadhuisplein 1.
The former district courthouse sits at Stadhuisplein 3, diagonally behind the city hall beside the Dommel river, and has been called the Designhuis since 2007 and Het Hornemann Huis in recent years.
Dutch Design Week lists that building as "Het Hornemann Huis (voormalig Designhuis)."
I keep the three names apart because the archive, the programs and the history all do.

blocks.x: The city hall took more than thirty years

r: The architecture center's Open Monumentendag brochure of 2020, written by René Erven and Peter Thoben, gives the fullest account I found. Eindhoven merged with its neighbors on January 1, 1920, and the council decided on December 28, 1928 to build a new city hall on a vacant field called the Studentenwei between the Wal and the Stratumseind. From 1929 the city's government used a large villa in Stratum as a temporary seat.

A public competition followed in 1938. Out of 110 entries four were picked, and a jury report dated May 11, 1939 favored the proposal of the Leiden architect J.A. (Jan) van der Laan, mainly for how it fitted the city. On April 16, 1940 the council approved his worked-out design, which carried the name Broleto. The war stopped the work.

After the war a part of the plan was built first as an emergency secretariat building. The first pile went in on August 2, 1949, the first stone was laid on October 18, 1950, and the mayor opened the building on January 19, 1952. It is a three-story brick building in a traditional style, and it now serves as a court building.

The main building changed a great deal in the meantime. Van der Laan finished a revised design in 1956, then told the council in 1957 that the 1939 concept might no longer be wise, and in 1958 presented a far more modern sketch with a ten-story office tower and a square-shaped ceremonial block around a central hall. The first pile of that building went in on November 4, 1965.
Van der Laan died in 1966, and the building was finished by his colleagues Kirch, Hermans and Van der Eerden, with the Eindhoven architect Hans Thomassen as project staff member.

Queen Juliana opened it on September 18, 1969, during the commemoration of 25 years since the city's liberation, and the mayor who received her had refused to approve the building plans in 1956 as minister of construction.

The next day, September 19, 1969, the Van Abbemuseum opened an exhibition with the model of the Cityplan by Van den Broek and Bakema, which the architecture center reads as a companion statement of the same modern course.

Four artists made the monumental works inside and on the building: Ad Dekkers (the wall relief in the council chamber), Peter Struycken (the tile relief near the lifts), André Volten (a hanging sculpture of 1,500 square meters of moving steel plates in the citizens' hall) and Arthur Spronken (the bronze figure on the facade). The carillon of 45 bells was first played at the opening.

The building was renovated in 2001 by architecten|en|en with buro Staal Christensen, whose main change was a glass roof, and again by the !MPULS alliance, delivered at the start of 2020, with a green entrance under the tower and the residents' desk moved back from the Stadskantoor on the Wal. The brochure says 95 percent of the materials released in the rebuild were reused.

blocks.x: The square: a field, a grid and a stage

r: The ground has its own history. The brochure says the Studentenwei lay where the city moat branched off the Dommel, near the Stratum watermill that had been in use since the fourteenth century. In 1812 a textile manufacturer bought the mill and built two factory buildings called Den Bouw, and the brochure says the first industrial steam engine in the Netherlands went into use there in 1820. The factory burned in 1896 and its ruins were cleared in 1928.
I treat the steam engine as the brochure's claim and did not check it elsewhere.

The square in front of the finished secretariat building was left as lawn for years. The Liberation Monument, designed by the sculptor Paul Gregoire with a stone surround by Van der Laan, was unveiled on September 18, 1954 and later moved about 50 meters to its present corner. The brochure dates the move to 1965 and the architecture center's own walking route dates it to 1969.

The present square was delivered in 1997. It measures about 50 by 50 meters and is divided in squares of about 10 meters, a grid that echoes the 1952 layout of concrete tiles, and five specially designed lamp posts stand for the five districts added to the city since the 1920 merger.

Light and art were the design principles, light because of Eindhoven's reputation as a city of lighting innovation, and art through a route called De Rode Loper, which the Van Abbemuseum started by inviting the American artists Lawrence Weiner and Matt Mullican to propose ideas.

One object on the square is easy to miss. Gerrit Rietveld designed a bus shelter that doubled as an advertising column for the city in 1962. Only one was built, around 1965 on the Hendrik Staetslaan, and it was moved to its current place in the 1990s (the brochure says 1990).

blocks.x: The courthouse that became the Designhuis

r: The building at Stadhuisplein 3 was designed as a district court by Johannes (Jo) Kruger for the national government's buildings agency, with design work in 1958 and 1959. It was finished in 1964, cost about two million guilders, a quarter of which went into the interior, and stood empty for months because the Danish furniture had been ordered too late. It was officially opened on May 21, 1965.

Inside, a large atrium carried a brick mosaic of 140 square meters by Theo van Amstel showing the biblical negotiation over the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah, which the Eindhovens Dagblad of the time called a symbol of modern case law. Judges and detainees shared one route through the building, while visitors, witnesses and counsel came through the central hall.

The court was abolished with the district courts in 2002, and in 2007 the building opened as the Designhuis after a conversion by the architect Peer van Ling. The mosaic disappeared behind a white wall.
The brochure names Lidewij Edelkoort, then head of the Design Academy Eindhoven, as the driving force.

The house was a Design Week venue from the start of its life. In October 2009 Bright reported that it showed "Talent 2009," Edelkoort's selection of 175 objects and installations by 2009 graduates of thirty European institutions, open until November 30, 2009. The same article reports that the municipality, the only grant-giver, had announced the house's closing in July and then let it organize two final exhibitions, and that the staff contracts would not be renewed after two years under Edelkoort.

The money story is in council papers. A party's published questions of February 1, 2013 and the college's answers say the municipality signed a five-year lease with Stichting Designhuis in 2007, that the co-financing from others fell short so the municipality became the only financier, and that from 2010 the municipality covered the building costs while others funded the content. A Vitra exhibition called "Hidden Heroes" was bought in for October 2010 to May 2011, and from summer 2011 the design institute Premsela funded exhibitions while Capital D, which the questioners describe as the organizer of Dutch Design Week, directed the volunteers.

The questioner's figures, including a rent debt of 210,000 euros, come from a political party and I cannot confirm them. The college's answer says only that the remaining debt was booked as a doubtful receivable.
After the design years the house held the local broadcaster Studio 040 and the Stichting Cultuur Eindhoven, per the 2020 brochure.

The Hornemann Huis, a remembrance center that tells the story of two Jewish brothers from Eindhoven murdered by the Nazis, moved in recently, according to the architecture center. Its article announces Open Monumentendag openings on Saturday, September 14 and Sunday, September 15, a weekend pairing that fits 2024, though the page text gives no year.
The Open Monumentendag entry for 2026 calls the building a municipal monument and lists it open on September 12 and 13, 2026.

blocks.x: What Design Week has done here, as far as the record shows

r: The earliest record I found is from 2009, when Bright lists the winning work of the Dutch Design Awards at the "Brainport Greenhouse" on Stadhuisplein, open 11:00 to 22:00 and until 20:00 on Sunday, October 25.
In 2013 a blog recap describes a display of XL posters with self-portraits made by parents and their children on the square.

For 2015 the evidence is the photo archive. The Stadhuis album has 14 photos and the Stadhuisplein album 16, and the photo pages credit Sjoerd Eickmans. I read those album pages on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen them in this pass. Inside the city hall they show wall posters of faces with captions, a table of small objects and a wooden clock. On the square they show a large steel wheel of colored balls, glass pavilions, a shipping container shop signed Kunstblok, a sign reading Treasure Light and a poster reading Design for Kids. Many show children, so I describe objects only.
I found no program text for these items, and no source says the glass pavilions were the Awards greenhouse of earlier years.

The 2016 record is fuller. IO+ reported on October 24, 2016 that the municipality's design show was in the city hall during Design Week, that Mieke Fiers of the social design office Tante Netty designed it, and that it played on the verb "Eindhoof." The show covered five themes, including the NRE terrain and a game for newcomers, and let visitors weigh in on a redesign of the Vestdijk.
The photos show stacked wooden walls with panels titled Fun op straat and Slim licht and a window reading Eindhoof je mee?

Outside, VPRO's tips of October 23, 2016 put the Solar Cabin by Bram Zondag and Arjan de Nooijer on the square, one of six winners of a competition called A Home Away From Home from the asylum seeker reception agency COA and the Rijksbouwmeester, Floris Alkemade.

For 2025 DDW's program page for touching cellulose_SENSE OF CRAFTING gives City Hall Square as the location and October 18 to 26, 2025 as the dates, free of charge, with students from TU Delft and TH Köln and visitors building a wooden EduCrafting Pavilion, with two daily introduction sessions. The archive album has 21 photos credited to Cleo Goossens in the titles.

For 2026 the picture is double. Dutch Design Week lists Het Hornemann Huis, open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 and free, with "Objects on Trial," a group exhibition by Bureau.parso and Meeseek in the former courthouse. The program text says the show uses the building's rooms of judgment, observation and waiting as a curatorial frame, with an Examination Room of samples and prototypes.

The program text does not mention the museum, and I draw no connection. On the square, DDW lists FIELD by Isabel + Helen, a wind-powered interactive installation of turbines on wheels, among eight large-scale installations that are free to visit.
The locations list also names a Raadzaal, the council chamber, at Stadhuisplein 1 and a "City Hall Square" entry.

The organizer describes why the square gets this use. Its 2025 call for Grand Projects names Stadhuisplein, Markt and Ketelhuisplein as high-visibility locations and calls them key squares that attract tens of thousands of visitors.
That is the organizer's description and I read it as one.

blocks.x: A square about to change

r: The city council adopted a master plan for the public space on September 30, 2025, which the project page says will turn the stony surroundings into a green, lively place over about ten years. The plan builds on a vision by Bygg Architecture & Design from November 2023 and aims to lead a branch of the Dommel across the square as a "Binnendommel" and to link green roofs of the surrounding buildings by four gates and bridges into a public lookout called the Belvedère. It prefers an underground link between garages that would remove the garage entrance, so cars no longer cross the square. Large events such as carnival, King's Day and a PSV championship celebration stay possible, with first estimates of 20 percent fewer visitors for King's Day and 25 percent fewer for the celebration.
Omroep Brabant put the last celebration at 19,000 supporters and the new capacity at about 15,000.
On August 25, 2026 it became known that the permit for Citywall, three mixed buildings on the north side with 330 homes, had been granted.

The idea of the square as an event stage is older than the plan. At a meeting of the architecture center on October 1, 2019, the city's supervising architect Winy Maas called the future square the "new dance floor" of Eindhoven.
The 2025 and 2026 Design Week programs fit that stage, but no source says they were chosen with it in mind.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: Short accounts say "Jan van der Laan." The architecture center's brochure and walking route give the fuller account: his Leiden office designed it, he died in 1966, and colleagues finished it. I describe it as designed by his office and completed by his successors.
When the courthouse became a municipal monument.

The architecture center's walking route of 2020 says it became one "this spring." The municipal gazette of January 28, 2026 says the college decided in 2015 to designate Stadhuisplein 3, that the decisions were sent to interested parties but by mistake not published for third parties, and that publication in 2026 repairs this.
The gazette is the primary text and I follow it for the 2015 decision. I cannot say whether the 2020 date refers to a second step.
Spelling and dates of the artists.

The architect of the courthouse is Kruger in the brochure and Krüger in the walking route, and the mosaic's artist Theo van Amstel is given as 1927 to 2010 in one and 1927 to 2004 in the other. I use Kruger and give no death year.
Whether the archive's years are the venue's years.

The archive holds albums for 2015, 2016 and 2025, and the sources above show Design Week on the square in 2009, 2013 and 2026 and in the Designhuis in 2009. The archive is therefore a sample of what photographers shot, and not a record of use.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I did not find a program for the 2015 items, a building-by-building account of the square before 1952, or a source for the Awards greenhouse in any year other than 2009. I did not find DDW programs at the city hall or on the square for 2010 to 2012, 2014 and 2017 to 2023, and the archive's single 2024 photo with Stadhuisplein in its title is not enough to say what it showed.

I cannot say how often Design Week used the Designhuis after 2011, which hand the city hall's show took in other years, or whether the 2015 glass pavilions were a greenhouse. I have not seen the council's own master plan, because the municipal website answered one request with an access refusal and I stopped using that host. I know it only through a project page of the Open Eindhoven site and the press.

If you stand on the square during Dutch Design Week 2026, look at the three buildings that face each other and ask which of them was built for the function it has now. When a courthouse becomes a design house, a design house becomes a remembrance center, and the remembrance center hosts an exhibition about judging objects, which of those uses would you say the building was made for?

posts.title: Strijp-S: a Philips company district, a Forbidden City, and a design week that filled it
posts.subtitle: The former Philips factory district in Eindhoven, followed through the national monument register, planning research, the owners' history and ten editions of official Dutch Design Week photo albums
posts.seoTitle: Strijp-S Eindhoven: Philips district to Design Week
posts.description: Strijp-S in Eindhoven, from a 1916 Philips glass factory and the Forbidden City to Dutch Design Week, with what the records do and do not show.

r: Philips began building on Strijp-S in 1916, decided in 1999 to leave it, sold it in a deal that two sources date to 2002 and two others date to 2004, and by 2007 Dutch Design Week was already using its Klokgebouw.

The common shorthand for Strijp-S is "the old Philips site that became a design district," and each half of that sentence hides a lot of paperwork. The site was a planned industrial landscape with a designer, a grid and a building code. It was closed by fences for decades. It was sold in stages, redeveloped in a partnership that nearly collapsed, and opened to the public in part through temporary uses before the permanent ones arrived. This essay follows that sequence through public sources: the national monument register, an urban-development research essay, the owners' history page, heritage and trade writing, contemporary press and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview. Dutch Design Week 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and I describe only what its pages list.
I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was built to do before asking what it does now. For Strijp-S the register answers that question with unusual precision.

blocks.x: A planned industrial landscape, south of the railway

r: The Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed describes the "Philipscomplex Strijp S" as a rectangular site south of the railway line. It says the need for a glass factory of Philips's own during the First World War was the first push toward a new complex, laid out next to the existing Philips buildings at Emmasingel and Philipsdorp. The layout was developed by A.I.J. de Broekert, who worked for Philips, and applied a high degree of rationality. From the 1920s the site was filled systematically with industrial buildings.

The register's description of the protected buildings is blunt about method. They are mostly three-aisle, multi-story factory buildings with a wide central street, built with a reinforced concrete skeleton, identical steel profiles from Krupp, pumice-concrete roof cassettes and long horizontal bands of daylight, a type developed by Philips. The register values the complex as an example of the industry's social and economic development, as a record of how large-scale industrial high-rise developed, and as a rare coherent industrial landscape.
That is the national government's reading, and it explains why the planners later treated the buildings as the backbone of the district.

The register also settles some dates that other sources blur. The Klokgebouw was built in two phases, in 1928 and 1929, to a design by de Broekert of the Philips engineering bureau, and includes a factory water tower.
The Veemgebouw was built in 1942 by the same engineering bureau and has expressionist elements.
Three multi-story factory buildings on the Leidingstraat, the "industrial boulevard" later called the Hoge Rug, date from 1930, 1929 and 1927, also to designs by de Broekert.

The Strijp-S owners' page says the Klokgebouw dates from 1929, a heritage article by Jan van Oudheusden gives 1928, and the architecture center's walking route says the Veemgebouw was finished in 1943.
I follow the register for all three.

blocks.x: What the owners say about the first decades

r: Strijp-S's own history page gives a plain timeline. Gerard Philips began making light bulbs in a small factory on the Emmasingel in 1891. Philips had its first Strijp-S factory built in 1916, a glass factory making glass balloons for lamps, so it would not depend on suppliers, followed by a cardboard factory, a gas factory and the Physics Laboratory, the NatLab. From 1928 the pace increased: the Klokgebouw, a factory for Philite, the Philips name for bakelite, then the appliance factories of the Hoge Rug, an engine room, a boiler house and the Veemgebouw. The page says Philips became completely self-sufficient on the site, "from raw material to finished product."

The NatLab date varies by source. The architecture center says the physicist Gilles Holst was appointed head of the laboratory in 1914 and that the research department moved into its own building in 1923, designed by Dirk Roosenburg.
Van Oudheusden dates the laboratory building to 1922.

I use 1923 and name the architecture center. The laboratory had a long reach. Strijp-S's history page says Queen Wilhelmina addressed the Dutch East Indies by wireless radio from the lab, that Einstein visited, and that the researcher Dick Raaijmakers took the first steps toward synthesizers there and made electronic music with them, a project it says Philips did not pursue.
The European Physical Society lists "The Philips NatLab, Eindhoven (2017)" among its Historic Sites.

The site was large, and the sources do not agree on how large. Strijp-S and the architecture center say 27 hectares, the Inventing Europe essay by Hans Schippers says 25 and Van Oudheusden says "about thirty."
I give 27 hectares and attribute it.

The district was also a target. On Sunday, December 6, 1942, the Royal Air Force bombed the Philips factories on the Emmasingel and on Strijp-S in the raid known as the Sinterklaas bombing, code name Operation Oyster. The national committee for commemoration says the raid was flown by 94 aircraft, that sixteen did not return, and that the monument unveiled on December 6, 2011 remembers about 150 civilian victims, since many bombs hit shops, homes and churches.
A local history site puts the civilian toll at about 138 dead and 161 injured, says 14 aircraft were lost, and says production was running again after about half a year.
The two accounts differ on the numbers and I give both. The raid shows that the factories were a wartime asset of the occupied city as well as a company campus.

In the 1970s, the owners' page says, some 10,000 people worked on the site every day, and Eindhoven nicknamed it the Forbidden City because fences and barriers surrounded it and you only got in with a pass.
Schippers adds that Philips, with its own schools, sports clubs and cultural institutions, was often called a state within the city.

Van Oudheusden repeats a story that the Torenallee boulevard was laid out as a sightline so that Frits Philips could see the Philips light tower from his house. He writes that it "appears" to be so, and I treat it as a legend.

blocks.x: Leaving, selling and the argument about 2002 and 2004

r: The departure was gradual. The architecture center places the turning point in the late 1980s, when Philips ran into economic trouble, and says that under Jan Timmer from 1990 the "Operation Centurion" reorganization closed factories and sold business units, and even the head office moved to Amsterdam.

A research essay by Simon van Zoest of the TU Delft program on urban transformation says Philips decided in 1999 to move its activities and that VolkerWessels won the tender for the area together with a pension fund investor. After the crisis that followed 2001 the investor withdrew, the whole transformation was in doubt, the municipality joined because it feared decay, and a public-private partnership of the municipality and VolkerWessels was born.
The renovation-oriented site Herbestemming adds that Philips organized a tender in 2001 and that the best plan came from VolkerWessels.

On the sale, each source is right about a different step. Strijp-S's history page says that in 2002 VolkerWessels and the municipality bought Strijp-S from Philips, that the fenced area was transferred and leased back to Philips, and that the partners set up Park Strijp Beheer.
The architecture center also gives 2002 and says the site of about 27 hectares was sold to the municipality and VolkerWessels partnership that year.
The Driehoek Strijp-S site says Philips sold the site to Park Strijp Beheer in 2004.
Herbestemming puts it in sequence: letter of intent in 2001, master plan in 2002, and in 2004 Park Strijp Beheer takes over the land from Philips, renting back the buildings Philips still used.

I read 2002 as the purchase agreement and 2004 as the transfer of the land. That reading comes from reconciling those sources and not from a deed, so I use "2002" only with the word "agreement" and say that the handover is dated 2004 elsewhere.

blocks.x: The plan, the partnership and the crisis

r: Strijp-S's history page says the plan was developed from 2002 to 2005 under Park Strijp Beheer, with the landscape architect Adriaan Geuze of West 8 drawing the urban plan and acting as supervisor. It says the zoning plan followed in 2005 and 2006, and that part of the old factories were designated as a municipal monument (the NatLab) and national monuments (the Hoge Rug and Klokgebouw).
Herbestemming dates the approved zoning plan to 2008 and a program for art and culture on Strijp-S to 2007.

The Van Zoest essay describes how the plan changed. It began as a fairly blueprint-driven plan with a lot of demolition and new building. While the first buildings were being demolished, friction grew inside the partnership, which led to a new governance structure with a "Board of Inspiration" of VolkerWessels, the municipality, the housing corporations and the supervisor Geuze. The 2008 credit crisis then forced changes, including a parking concept and more heritage preservation, and a large skate hall that was meant to be temporary became permanent.

Strijp-S's own page agrees on the outcome: in 2012 and 2013 the demolition of many Philips factories was postponed and later canceled, and development in four phases moved from the edge toward the center.
Van Zoest's account says the area now holds about 500 new residents and 700 companies, a figure from 2019.

The housing corporations carried much of the early reuse. The architecture center says the housing corporation Trudo developed the buildings around the Driehoek, including the Klokgebouw, and that old factory buildings became open studios, music stages, restaurants, schools and small shops, with some housing. Herbestemming says Woonbedrijf built the first new homes, with construction starting in 2010 and the first residents arriving at the end of 2012.
Herbestemming says the city bought the Klokgebouw in 2006 and that its transformation to studios, a music venue and event halls was delivered in 2010.

The Strijp-S history page says that, in the latest phase, new buildings adapt to monuments: Trudo's Haasje Over project is built over the former Area51 hall, and the partners plan 2,000 more homes and 25,000 square meters for creative businesses.

blocks.x: When Design Week arrived

r: The owners' history page says the 2005 and 2006 consortium investment "resulted in Dutch Design Week choosing Strijp-S as its new home."

I found independent evidence from 2007. A car magazine's news item of October 15, 2007 says the Citroën C-Buggy would be shown for the first time in the Netherlands at the Design On Wheels show in the Klokgebouw Strijp-S during Design Week from October 20 to 28.
In 2009 Bright lists a Design On Wheels stand in the Klokgebouw, a student show on Strijp-S and its own stand in hall 4 of the Klokgebouw.
By 2012 Bright reported that the biggest concentration of young talent had moved out of the Klokgebouw to a video lab elsewhere on Strijp-S.
I did not find a source for the first year. The history page's "2005 and 2006" is the owners' account, and 2007 is the earliest date I can support from outside.

blocks.x: What the photo archive shows, year by year

r: The albums below are the ones read for the earlier Strijp-S research on October 6, 2026, and I did not reopen them in this pass. They show the district as a sequence of squares, not factories.

Ketelhuisplein has albums for 2015 (33 photos), 2016 (67), 2017 (38), 2018 (20) and 2019 (28). Titles name Cleo Goossens, Tommy Köhlbrugge, Almicheal Fraay, Dick Rennings, Ruud Balk, Max Kneefel and Oscar Vinck. The pictures show the square from above, banners, stages, a green ABN AMRO box, a train-carriage pavilion and, in 2019, a raised wooden pavilion and a BioBaseCamp.

The 2021 album (38 photos, October 16 and 17, 2021) shows timber houses, and 2023 (58) shows market tents and greenhouses. In 2022 the album is for Trudotorenplein (43 photos), beside residential towers. In 2024 the subject is Microlab Hall (17 photos), and for 2025 the album is an introduction with 6 photos of orange and purple pavilions. No album in this set covers 2020.

The Strijp-S building pages describe the Trudo Tower as a 70-meter tower by Stefano Boeri Architetti with 125 social housing lofts, a new building with no Philips function, and Microlab as flexible workspace in the former Philips SFH building.

DDW's own 2026 location list groups about forty entries under Strijp-S, among them Area 51, Bakkie 040, a Community Square, Plug in City, the Ketelhuisplein Greenhouse, the Klokgebouw, Matchbox, MU Hybrid Art House, Natlab, a passage at the Trudo tower, Radio Royaal, SintLucas, Skybar Microlab and VEEM floor 8.
The count and the names are DDW's grouping and not a statement about ownership or history.

blocks.x: The doubts about the success story

r: The success story has a counter-voice, thin but present. In March 2026 Stadszaken reported a Sectie-C tenant who hoped that site would not go the way of Strijp-S, where "ruimte voor creativiteit onder druk" is said by those involved to have come under pressure. That is a second-hand characterization inside an article about another place, and I did not find a study or a named case that supports it.
The Van Zoest essay calls the transformation widely seen as successful and notes that it won a national renovation prize and a developers' award.
The question of who the district's cheap space serves today is not one the sources I opened answer.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: 2002 (owners, architecture center), 2004 (Driehoek, Herbestemming for the land transfer). Reconciled as agreement and handover, but not settled by a primary document.

Settled by the national register: Klokgebouw 1928 and 1929 in two phases, Veemgebouw 1942, Hoge Rug 1927, 1929 and 1930. The architecture center's separate dating of the Hoge Rug buildings (the SK building to 1928, SBP to 1930, SAN to 1929) differs for one of them, so I give the register's set only.

Herbestemming and Strijp-S's own Glasgebouw page say the very first light bulbs were made in the Glasgebouw; Strijp-S's history page puts the first bulbs in the Emmasingel factory in 1891, before any Strijp-S building. I follow the history page and leave the Glasgebouw claim out.
25 hectares (Schippers), 27 (owners, architecture center), about 30 (Van Oudheusden). Not settled.
Much of the district's history comes from the owners' own page and a housing-corporation partner's site. Where I could, I set them beside the register and the research essay.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have not read the sale or transfer deeds, the 2001 tender documents or the master plan itself, and I have not seen the council's papers. The council information site was not reachable in this pass. I cannot say what Design Week used on Strijp-S before 2007, why the photo selection has no 2020 album, or what the 2025 introduction album's street is called. I did not reopen the Flickr albums, so counts and credits carry their October 6 date.

I do not know how many creative tenants have left or stayed since the first temporary uses, and I could not verify the claim about creative space under pressure. I also have no source for the 1916 factory's later fate or for which buildings were demolished in the first phase beyond the general statements above.

If you walk Strijp-S during Dutch Design Week 2026, find a building on the register and read its plate against the dates in this essay. When a district's year of sale depends on whether you mean the agreement or the handover, which date would you put on the wall?

posts.title: TAC: a Philips office from 1930, a temporary art centre from 2004, and a building it now says it owns
posts.subtitle: A former Philips office building near the stadium in Eindhoven, followed through the venue's own timeline, a building-history researcher, trade and local press, and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
posts.seoTitle: TAC Eindhoven: Philips office to art centre
posts.description: The Temporary Art Centre building in Eindhoven, from a Philips office of about 1930 to a Dutch Design Week venue, with what the records do and do not show.

r: The building that houses the Temporary Art Centre in Eindhoven was built for Philips around 1930, held a school, sales offices, a wartime head office, a staff shop and a museum depot, and in 2025 reopened in part after a renovation that tore down another part of it.

The Temporary Art Centre publishes a long timeline on its own site, and most of the building's history rests on it. I looked for other sources and found a building-history researcher, a demolition contractor and TAC's own pages on its renovation, which let me check parts of the timeline. The result is a better-supported building history and a less certain account of the organization. This essay follows both. I use public sources only: TAC's pages, the researcher's note, trade pages on the renovation, a design magazine's 2012 report, This is Eindhoven, the Dutch Design Week pages and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview. Dutch Design Week 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and I describe only what its pages list.
I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was built to do before asking what it does now. For this building the list of earlier uses is long, which is the point of the exercise.

blocks.x: An office building for a lamp company

r: TAC's timeline begins in 1927, when Philips submitted a planning application for an office building. It lists the years 1930 to 1992 as "Philips," a Philips ULO school and training center for office staff in 1933 and 1934, and the Dutch Sales Department from 1930 to 1964.
A building-history researcher, Gerrit Korenberg, gives the independent anchor. His project note says the office building was built in 1930 for the N.V. Philips Gloeilampenfabriek.

A 1927 application and a building in use by 1930 fit together, and two sources agree on 1930. I treat 1930 as the year the building came into use and 1927 as the year the plan was filed. The researcher's note gives no exact day and no architect.

The timeline continues with the war. It lists the German authorities occupying the building from 1940 to 1945. It says Frits Philips established his office there from 1942, and that the building served as a temporary Philips head office from 1943 to 1964.
Korenberg's note explains why: when the Philips head office was hit in a bombing in 1942, the directors were housed in this building, which got a new main entrance and upgraded offices.
The bombing was most likely the RAF raid of December 6, 1942 on the Philips factories on the Emmasingel and Strijp-S, though the researcher's note does not name the date.
The two sources differ on the years. The timeline says the temporary head office ran from 1943, and the researcher says the directors moved after the 1942 bombing. I give both.

The temporary arrangement ended with a new building. The architecture center says the Philips Nederland office building VB on the Boschdijk was opened on December 29, 1964, after four years of construction, and gathered about 1,300 employees who had worked at five locations in Eindhoven.
The TAC timeline ends the Dutch Sales Department and the temporary head office in 1964.
I read those as the same event seen from two ends, which is my inference and not a statement in either source.

blocks.x: Offices, a canteen, a staff shop and a gap

r: After 1964 the timeline lists a housing and land company and a Philips canteen until 1988, then social services, a personnel department, a housing office, a tax advisory office, sports and recreation services from 1965 onward, and from 1978 a support fund, a travel agency, a reproduction department and the works council's office. It gives the staff shop 1972 to 1992.
Korenberg also mentions the staff shop from about 1972.
The demolition contractor's page, describing the renovation, calls the part being demolished the place "where the Philips staff shop was once housed."
One entry matters for the building's present shape: in 1985 a large section along the Gagelstraat was demolished.

The building TAC took over in 2004 was therefore already smaller than the one Philips built, and the renovation of the 2020s removed another part. The timeline says the building became vacant in 1992.

blocks.x: The Van Abbemuseum years, and a date that disagrees

r: From 1995 to 2003 the timeline says the Van Abbemuseum used the building as a depot and as its temporary location during the rebuilding of its own premises.
Korenberg writes that the museum was temporarily housed there from 1995 to 2002 and that TAC has been there since 2002.

The energy company Ennatuurlijk, in an August 2025 news item about reconnecting the building to its heat network, also says it has been a cultural breeding ground since 2002, and describes the building as originally built as a Philips office in the 1930s.
The museum's own page on its director Jan Debbaut says the museum moved to a temporary location in 1995, without naming the building, and stayed until 2002, which matches the researcher's dates.
The disagreement is a year on the museum's departure and two years on TAC's arrival, since TAC's own timeline says it became a foundation, an organization and a physical space in 2004.
TAC's text on the Petri complex adds that its original plans for TAC Living date from 2003, "a year before we moved into the TAC building."
I follow TAC for its own move, 2004, and report 2002 as the date two outside sources use. The outside sources may be counting from the first use of part of the building, but none says so.

blocks.x: How an art centre began in a pub

r: TAC's own words are that it "was born at a pub bar in 1999," as a concept scribbled on a beer coaster.

In 2004 it became a foundation, an organization and a physical space, a base for emerging artists, designers, musicians, theater makers and architects who move on as they grow, which the timeline gives as the reason for the word temporary.
This is Eindhoven repeats that explanation: at TAC they do not say contemporary but temporary, because that is how the Temporary Art Centre began.
The early years produced a magazine. TAC's about page says that after just over a year it published VAN TAC, in several editions between 2004 and 2008.

The timeline records a street festival, Via Ventosa, launched in 2005, and the hope in that year, with the municipality, the Ventoseflat association and the housing corporation Woonbedrijf, to redevelop the neighboring Ventoseflat. It says the plans for what it called the Petri complex, a breeding ground for art with living space, were put on hold in 2006 and that new plans were revived in 2017.

blocks.x: Design Week at TAC

r: I found one independent early record of TAC at Design Week. In October 2012 Bright wrote that TAC, "next to the Philips Stadium," always produces surprises, in a roundup of that year's venues.
TAC's home page lists Dutch Design Week 2026, October 17 to 25, among its events.

The Flickr archive begins in 2015. I read its album pages for the earlier version of this research on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen them in this pass, so the counts and names below carry that date. Six editions have TAC albums, seven albums and 145 photos in all.

The 2015 albums hold 9 photos by Cleo Goossens, six of them titled Overzicht, and 17 photos by Nick Bookelaar of a Late Night Bingo Show. The 2016 album has 16 photos with number titles, 2017 has 12 with titles naming Sint Joost and WDKA, and 2018 is the largest with 56, of which the earlier pass could read 24: lamps, mineral samples and a staged bedroom. The 2019 album has 13, nine of them titled WATTBA, with a banner reading What a Time to Be Alive. The 2020 album has 22 photos by Max Kneefel of installed rooms with almost no visitors.
The 2020 week ran online as well as offline, with visits by appointment, according to CLICKNL, which may explain the empty rooms.

blocks.x: The move out and the rebuild

r: TAC's timeline says that in 2021, with the renovation about to begin, TAC moved with most of its members to a former school building at Kronehoefstraat 30A and another group moved to Sectie-C.

A TAC page on its future describes public events at three other locations during the renovation, including exhibitions at the old address, programs at United Cowboys on Kleine Berg and a stage at the High Tech Campus.

The plans and the money changed along the way. The same page says the building was originally going to be demolished entirely, that TAC found a partner in Focus Real Estate and that the decision was to preserve it in part. It names the architecture firm KCAP and Atelier Boetzkes in the preliminary design, with 80 studios for 200 artists and 230 new homes, and says the iconic entrance will be kept. It expected the move back in early 2024 and the housing a year later.

The contractor who carried out the demolition says a residential tower of about 249 apartments for Woonbedrijf is being realized by Huybregts-Relou, that a part of the historic building will be demolished entirely and that the other part is kept as a cultural center.

The 230 and 249 figures differ and I give both with their sources. A Brainport Eindhoven page on the national Regio Deal lists TAC Vastgoed B.V. as the beneficiary of a project running from October 1, 2019 to December 31, 2025, with a national contribution of 3,100,000 euros, regional co-financing of at least 7,571,429 euros and a total of 10,671,429 euros, with Focus Real Estate and the municipality as partners. It describes the plan as keeping about 4,800 square meters of studios, makerspaces, exhibition space and hospitality in place and as giving TAC a self-standing, independent form, "TAC 2.0."

An architecture firm's page on the same project says TAC had the old Philips building on loan from the municipality, that the original plans for the area had no place for it, and that an agreement with the municipality now keeps TAC on the site in exchange for creating affordable housing.
Ennatuurlijk says the renovation started in 2024 and was carried out by TAC Vastgoed B.V., and expected activities in the building again at the end of 2025.
TAC's timeline says the first phase was completed in 2025, with the exhibition spaces, the Ballroom and the Vault, ready for their first exhibitions.
TAC's home page says that on November 5 (the year is not shown) it became official that the building belongs to TAC, and invites visitors to the first two exhibition spaces.

An Open Eindhoven news item of December 2, 2025, read for the earlier research and not reopened because that host later answered with an access refusal, reports the opening of the renewed TAC with about 80 studios in 4,800 square meters and TAC Living with 249 apartments.

blocks.x: What the Design Week listing says for 2026

r: DDW lists TAC for October 17 to 25, 2026, with opening hours from 11:00 until 21:00 or 23:00 on most days and until 20:00 on the last Sunday. The text says TAC offers promising makers the chance to develop and present their work, with more than 100 young designers, artists and musicians in 60 studios.
The location page shows the address Vonderweg 1, while TAC's own home page gives Ventoselaan 1 for its office and studios and its exhibitions.
TAC's future page uses Vonderweg 1 for exhibitions during the renovation, so both addresses are TAC's own.
The studio count is also TAC's own on both sides: 60 on the Design Week page and 80 on TAC's about page.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: When the building came into use.
The 1927 filing and the 1930 use fit together, and the researcher's 1930 settles it as far as one independent note can.
After the 1942 bombing (researcher) or from 1943 (TAC's timeline). Not settled.
2004 (TAC) or 2002 (researcher and the energy company). I follow TAC and flag the rest.
60 or 80 studios, 230 or 249 homes. Different dates and different documents, not settled.
Vonderweg 1 and Ventoselaan 1 are both used by TAC.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have not seen the building's heritage assessment, a drawing or an architect's name for the 1930 office, or a record of its monument status. I did not look for archive or heritage records beyond those named above. I cannot say what TAC showed at Design Week before 2015 beyond the 2012 mention, why the photo archive has no TAC album after 2020, or what the 32 unseen photos of the 2018 album show. I also have no source for the exact date and terms on which TAC acquired the building.

If you walk past the building during Dutch Design Week 2026, look for the entrance that survived the demolition and ask what the rest of the facade once belonged to. When a building has been a school, a head office, a staff shop and a museum depot before it became an art centre called temporary, which of those names would you leave on it?
