posts.title: The Van Abbemuseum: a cigar maker's gift to the city, ninety years of directors, and a Design Week partner since at least 2009
posts.subtitle: A museum from 1936 in Eindhoven, followed through its own history pages, the national monument register, the Design Week program archive and seven editions of official photo albums
posts.seoTitle: Van Abbemuseum Eindhoven and Dutch Design Week
posts.description: The Van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven, from a cigar maker's 1936 gift to a Dutch Design Week venue, with its directors, building and what the records do and do not show.

r: The Van Abbemuseum opened on April 18, 1936 in a building paid for by a cigar manufacturer, and by 2009 it was one of the places a Dutch Design Week pass opened.

The usual way to read a museum in a design-week archive is as a list of exhibition titles, and that is how the photo albums present it. The museum's own history gives the titles a context. Six directors, a rebuilt building and a long relationship with the Design Academy Eindhoven sit behind them. This essay uses public sources only: the museum's own pages, the national monument register, the architecture center's heritage writing, Design Week's program archive, design and trade press, and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview. Dutch Design Week 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and I describe only what its pages list.

I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was built to do before asking what it does now. This building was built to hold paintings, was later joined to a tower for a growing collection, and in 2026 is described by its director as a sundial.

blocks.x: A gift from a cigar manufacturer

r: The museum is named after H.J. van Abbe, whom it describes as the cigar manufacturer who financed the building and set aside a sum for purchases and running costs in the first years.
The national monument register adds that he gave the museum to the city of Eindhoven together with paintings and a sum of money for buying art.

The register dates the building to 1936 and names A.J. Kropholler (1882 to 1973) as the architect. It describes a square plan of 40 by 40 meters, dark red brick, copper roofs, a clock tower over the front, and two rearing horses by the sculptor John Raedecker beside the steps.
The architecture center's walking route says the building went up in the years 1933 to 1935 and opened in 1936, and gives Kropholler's birth year as 1881.
I follow the register for 1882 and note the difference.

The museum says it officially opened on April 18, 1936 with the exhibition Hedendaagsche Nederlandse Kunst, Contemporary Dutch Art. At the opening the first director, Dr. W.J.A. Visser, hoped the museum would become "part of the living community." The name was a problem from the start: the inscription "Stedelijk Van Abbemuseum" was put on a memorial stone by mistake just before the opening, and because the public already used that name, the council changed it officially on April 10.

blocks.x: Directors and what they bought

r: The museum's own pages sketch the directors in some detail, and the sketches explain why its exhibitions look the way they do. Edy de Wilde, who took over in July 1946 at the age of 26, laid the foundation of the modern collection, dismissed the roughly 70 prewar paintings as incomplete, and in 1952 bought Chagall's Hommage à Apollinaire as the start of a core collection. Picasso's Femme en vert, bought for 114,000 guilders, caused public commotion.

Jean Leering, director from April 1964, was a structural engineer interested in architecture, urban planning and design. His program mixed New York artists with historical retrospectives of El Lissitzky, Moholy-Nagy, Van Doesburg and Tatlin. In 1968 he bought 86 works by Lissitzky, which the museum says made its holdings the largest outside Russia.
That ranking is the museum's claim and I did not check it elsewhere.
Rudi Fuchs, director from February 1975, argued for the autonomy of art and turned the program toward German, Austrian and Italian artists.

Jan Debbaut took over in January 1988. In 1990 the architect Abel Cahen was given the assignment to draw up a rough plan for a new building. In 1995, in anticipation, the museum moved to a temporary location under the slogan Van AbbeMUSEUM entr'acte, where it stayed until 2002.
Charles Esche led the museum from August 2004 to 2024, and Defne Ayas took over in September 2025, ahead of the museum's 90th birthday in spring 2026.

One exhibition connects the museum to the city around it. On September 19, 1969, the day after Queen Juliana opened the new city hall, the museum opened an exhibition with the model of the Cityplan by the Rotterdam firm Van den Broek and Bakema, which the architecture center reads as a companion statement to the new city hall's modern course.

blocks.x: An old building and a new tower

r: The register describes the museum as a monument, and a 2003 rebuild joined it to something very different. The museum's architecture page says the listed old building by Kropholler was renovated and integrated in 2003 into Abel Cahen's design for a new building. The new part has a 27-meter tower with inward-sloping walls, a facade of gray slate from Lapland, interiors by Maarten van Severen and a front garden by Piet Oudolf. The landscape architects H+N+S widened the Dommel into an "inner lake," and John Körmeling's footbridge, a small pink house with lighted words on its roof, followed in 2006.
The two buildings carry different addresses: the register lists the old building at Bilderdijklaan 10, and the museum and Dutch Design Week give Stratumsedijk 2.
The first is the monument's registered address and the second is the museum's address today.

blocks.x: Design Week at the museum, year by year

r: The earliest record I found is from 2009. Bright's guide to that year's Design Week says a pass of 22 euros gave access to the Design Academy, the Dutch Design Awards greenhouse, TU/e, the Van Abbemuseum, the Klokgebouw and the Designhuis.
In 2012 Bright reported that the DOEN materials prize had landed, less accessibly than usual, in the Van Abbemuseum.

The Flickr archive, which begins in 2015, holds albums for seven editions, 193 photos in all. I read those album pages for the earlier research on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen them in this pass.

Beyond Generations, October 7 to November 5, was a group exhibition of work by designers of different generations who studied at the Design Academy Eindhoven, which was founded in 1947 and was approaching its 75th anniversary. The curator was Annemartine van Kesteren of the Boijmans Van Beuningen museum. The museum's record says the show used eight frames of thinking, each marked by a dialog between two iconic products set beside a work from the museum's collection. The opening on October 7 was addressed by Esche and by a member of the academy's executive board.
The album has 26 photos by Tommy Köhlbrugge.

The Design Academy's page says its GEO-DESIGN platform, produced with the Van Abbemuseum, began in October 2018 with GEO-DESIGN: Alibaba, for which nine graduates researched Alibaba's operating model and its effect on design.
The album has 17 photos titled GEO-DESIGN.
GEO-DESIGN: Junk, which DDW's program archive calls a city-wide exhibition produced in collaboration with the museum, showed 18 projects by academy alumni.
The album has 20 photos with dates of October 19, 23 and 27.
Interior Design listed New Melancholy by Lidewij Edelkoort as a double exhibition between Kazerne and the Van Abbemuseum, showing pensive work from the collections of Edelkoort and the museum.
The two albums hold 43 photos and name both venues, so I cannot say which room is which.

The museum's DDW program item "De collectie is... De Edelkoort collectie" ran from October 8 to November 6, 2022 in ten rooms of the old building. It put design objects from Edelkoort's private collection beside contemporary art from the museum, with pieces by Maarten Baas, Jurgen Bey, Nacho Carbonell, Piet Hein Eek, Hella Jongerius and Studio Job, and a second showing at Kazerne until spring 2023.

museum.nl lists the museum's Design Week program from October 19 to 27, 2024: the exhibition Soils, complemented by work from Design Academy students, Jeroen Erosie's living mural Alternative Entrance and four stations by the collective De Onkruidenier about how design shapes a food such as the tomato.
The album has seven photos by Boudewijn Bollmann.
The archive's one museum album is titled for a visit by Queen Máxima and holds 45 photos by Max Kneefel with file names dated October 16, 2025.

DDW's press release says that evening she opened the 25th Dutch Design Week, and that before the opening she visited the exhibition Bridging Minds, 100x design for change at the museum. Dutch Design Week co-founder Miriam van der Lubbe curated it, with about 100 designers and artists including Formafantasma and Klarenbeek and Dros.

DDW lists the museum open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 on October 17 to 25, with a DDW ticket required, and a program item called Museum as Sundial. The text says Ayas conceived it as an exercise in reorientation, that the building, designed ninety years ago in relation to the sun, becomes a sundial with the central gallery as a point of orientation, and that it brings together contemporary art, design, archaeology and play, with participants including Kiki & Joost, Gala Porras-Kim, Paul Panhuysen and John Körmeling.
The claim about the 1936 design is the museum's own, and I could not check it against the register, which says nothing about the sun.

blocks.x: What the pattern shows

r: Across those years the Design Academy appears in the program of 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2024, and Edelkoort in 2020 and 2022.

The architecture center's brochure also names Edelkoort as the driving force behind the Designhuis in 2007, and her collection show at the museum had a second showing at Kazerne, so the museum's Design Week program is partly the same small circle seen from different buildings.

That is a pattern in the program, and the albums only record it. A separate venue with a similar name belongs to a different story: DDW lists the van Abbehuis, at Bilderdijklaan 19, as the former villa of the van Abbe family and an experimental project space for some 200 artists in recent years. The page does not mention the museum.
The archive holds a 2023 album titled Albert van Abbehuis with 9 photos and a 2025 album titled Van Abbe Huis with 8, and I count neither among the museum's.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: 1882 in the register, 1881 in the architecture center's route. I follow the register.
Bilderdijklaan 10 (register, the historic building) against Stratumsedijk 2 (the museum and DDW, the present entrance). Both are right for different things.

The museum says it moved to a temporary location in 1995 and stayed until 2002, without naming the building. The Temporary Art Centre's timeline says the museum used its building from 1995 to 2003, and a building-history note on that building says 1995 to 2002. The museum's own dates agree with the note.
Whether the museum is a Philips site.
No source I opened links it to Philips. The founder was a cigar manufacturer.

The museum's own pages say "one of the first public museums for contemporary art to be established in Europe," while the Design Week 2026 location text says "one of the leading museums." These are the museum's words in different places, and I attribute them rather than rank them.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I did not find the museum's own press releases for 2018, 2019 or 2025, because its press pages answered not found, so exact dates for those shows and the dates of Bridging Minds rest on Design Week's pages. I cannot say why the archive has no museum album for 2021 or 2023, which galleries held the 2020 show, or whether the van Abbehuis has any tie to the museum. I did not reopen the Flickr albums, so counts and credits carry their October 7 date.

If you visit during Dutch Design Week 2026, check which title DDW's listing gives for the museum before you go. When a program calls a 1936 brick building a sundial, which of its own earlier uses would you ask it to show you first?

posts.title: The Veemgebouw: a Philips warehouse with a television mast, a food hall and car park, and a festival home since 2019
posts.subtitle: The Philips warehouse on Strijp-S followed through the national monument register, an architecture journal, the owners' pages, the organizers' own sites and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Veemgebouw Eindhoven: Philips warehouse to festival home
posts.description: The Veemgebouw on Strijp-S, from a 1942 Philips warehouse and television mast to a food hall, car park, housing and Dutch Design Week home, with what the records do and do not show.

r: The Veemgebouw in Eindhoven was built in the early 1940s as a Philips warehouse, carried an experimental television antenna in the late 1940s, and has been converted into a food hall, a car park, housing and the home of a media-art festival that has used it in most Design Weeks since 2019.

A building's history gets tidier every time someone retells it, and the Veemgebouw is a good place to watch that happen. The Dutch Design Week photo albums call it VEEM, the monument register calls it the "veemgebouw," and the architects who rebuilt it call it Veemgebouw. This essay follows it through those documents and through the organizers' own sites for the exhibitions inside it. I use public sources only. It reports no visit and no interview. Dutch Design Week 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and I describe only what its pages list.
I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was built to do before asking what it does now. For a warehouse the answer is simple, which makes the later answers easier to compare.

blocks.x: Built as the end of the line

r: The national monument register describes the Veemgebouw as built in 1942 to a design of the Philips engineering bureau, with expressionist elements, on the west edge of the Philips site along the Beukenlaan, in line with a series of concrete warehouses. It is one of the buildings of the register's Philips complex on Strijp-S.
Caruso St John, the architects who later rebuilt it, say the building was constructed in 1943 and is the most prominent of the large industrial buildings at the heart of the site.
The architecture center's walking route says it was finished during the war, in 1943.
Strijp-S's history page describes it as a new building of the war years with typical rounded corners, meant for storing parts and products.
I credit 1942 to the register and note that the other two sources say 1943, which may mean completion and not the start.

The Architects' Journal, in a building study of October 24, 2022, explains what the building was for. The line of factory blocks on Strijp-S followed Philips's motto "from sand to customer," raw materials entering at one end and finished goods leaving at the other, and the Veem, short for Veemgebouw, was the end of the line, where finished products were stored before distribution. It stood next to the ring road and a railhead. On its tenth floor sat offices, marked by an illuminated mast and resembling a ship's bridge, where executives worked beside a showroom, which in the journal's words gave the building a representative role.
The structure is a grid of thick concrete columns with splayed tops at six-meter centers, ceilings only 2.8 meters high and floors over 35 meters deep.
The monument register describes the building as of general interest as part of the coherent Philips industrial landscape.

blocks.x: The mast and the first Dutch television

r: The story that a first Dutch television broadcast came from the Veem's roof is too big. The supported version is smaller and still good. Omroep Brabant reported in 2021 that Philips sent experimental programs, called Philips Experimentele Televisie, three evenings a week from 1948 to 1951, 264 test broadcasts in all, with an antenna on the roof of the Veemgebouw that reached forty kilometers. People who had received a set from Philips, often higher Philips staff, and radio dealers with a set in the window could watch. The presenter was often a Philips secretary, and the first live football match on television, PSV against EVV, was shown in 1950.
The same article says the first national broadcast, on October 2, 1951, came from a studio in Bussum rented by Philips, which was more central and nearer to Hilversum.
The Canon van Nederland confirms the date and that Philips began making programs itself in 1948, reachable only near Eindhoven.
The architecture center adds that a wooden mast stood on the roof for years and was used for the experimental television broadcasts of the late 1940s.

blocks.x: Philips leaves, Trudo arrives

r: The Architects' Journal says Philips closed manufacturing on the site in 1996 and that the site was sold in 2002 to Park Strijp Beheer, the partnership of the city and VolkerWessels.

Strijp-S's own page for the building says the housing corporation Trudo acquired the Veem in 2009 and decided to redevelop it, and that because the building has low floor heights and small windows it is less suitable for housing, so Trudo chose a mixed use.
The journal gives a different order: it says Trudo decided in 2007 to hold an ideas competition for the building, which Caruso St John won.
The architects' own page agrees with 2007 and dates the project 2007 to 2022, with the competition's first prize.

I cannot say how an ideas competition came in 2007 for a building the owners' page says Trudo bought in 2009. The owners' page may be dating a formal purchase, and Trudo's own statement in the journal says it has owned the building for a long time.

The design idea was to leave the deep warehouse as it was and add three floors of housing on top. The journal says the housing design dates to 2011 and was redesigned as penthouse apartments that year, after which the project was put on ice for several years; the retrofit of the main building went ahead in 2015 and work on the housing began in 2019.
Trudo's project leader says the ground-floor market hall was realized in 2015 and that an opportunity for the housing arose in 2020 when the facades were being maintained.

Strijp-S's page says Trudo had the three layers built in 2021, and Trudo's page says it realized the 39 homes in 2021 and 2022, replacing 11,500 window panes in the facade work and holding the building since 2009.
The completion year the journal gives is 2022.

What the building holds now is well documented. The Strijp-S page lists a supermarket, a restaurant, specialty shops and a brewery on the ground floor, then a parking garage, a VR experience center and several floors used for pop-up exhibitions during Dutch Design Week.

The architects describe a food market hall across the whole width of the deep ground floor, nine middle floors holding parking for six hundred cars for residents of the whole site, and offices and about forty apartments around a landscaped courtyard on top.

The journal explains the car park: Dutch law then required 1.2 parking spaces per new home, and reusing the storage floors for car storage needed minimal conversion. It reports a gross floor area of 30,000 square meters and a construction cost of 55 million euros.

The count of homes varies. Strijp-S and Trudo's own page say 39 homes, made of 19 studios, 19 maisonettes and one house, the architects say forty apartments, and Trudo's project leader in the journal says 38 studios and maisonettes.

The Dutch renovation platform NRP's page for the building carries a jury report that praises the care of the renovation and the idea of turning a warehouse into a car park, and says parking was expanded from three floors to five, with the remaining floors left to temporary tenants.
The architects' news page lists a RIBA International Award and the gold prize of the Erich Mendelsohn Award for brick architecture, in the housing and residential category.
I did not find the years on that page.

blocks.x: Earlier Design Weeks, and the festival that moved in

r: Core77's report on Dutch Design Week 2015, dated November 16, 2015, places the Dutch Design Awards exhibition, the show "In No Particular Order" and "Transnatural" in the Veemgebouw, and shows a view of the rest of Strijp-S from an eighth-floor corner window of the "storage building."
So the building was a Design Week venue by 2015 at least, a year before the archive's first VEEM album.

The most important fact for Design Week after that is a festival. Manifestations, a media-art, technology and fashion festival, says on its own sites that it has held its exhibition at the Veem during Dutch Design Week in several years. Its 2019 edition lists October 19 to 27, 2019, free admission, daily 11:00 to 18:00, at the Veemgebouw.
Its 2020 site says the 2020 edition was virtual, on its own site, on ddw.nl and in virtual worlds, and hoped to be physical again later at Sectie-C.
Its 2021 site says the 2021 edition would take place in the Melkhal at De Caai, the former Campina site, and online.
From 2022 the sites name the Veem: October 22 to 30, 2022, October 21 to 29, 2023, October 19 to 27, 2024 and October 18 to 26, 2025, each announced as running at the Veem "and longer."

For 2026 the festival's site announces October 17 to 25, 2026 at the Veem, and Dutch Design Week's own location page lists "VEEM floor 8 - home of Manifestations," free of charge, at Torenallee 100, open from 11:00 to 18:30 most days, with more than 50 participants, a food court and a brewery downstairs.
The 2026 theme on the festival's site is MUTE, about censorship and taboo.

Crafts Council Nederland has also shown at the Veem. Its pages record the exhibition HOW&WOW at the Veem during Dutch Design Week 2017, a studio version, HOW&WOW Studio, at the Veem in 2018, and a group exhibition from October 19 to 27, 2019 at the Veem.

blocks.x: What the photo archive shows, edition by edition

r: The official archive holds albums naming VEEM for six editions between 2016 and 2024, 265 photos in all. I read those album pages for the earlier research on October 6 and 7, 2026 and did not reopen them in this pass, so the counts and credits below carry those dates.

The 2016 album is titled Dutch Invertuals @ Veem, with 9 photos by Nick Bookelaar. This is the one row I now doubt. Domus gave the address of the Dutch Invertuals show "Power Play" at Design Week 2016 as Fuutlaan 12b, and the Neon Moiré guide gave NS Loods / studio Edhv, October 22 to 30, 2016.

I found no source that puts that show at the Veem, and I cannot reopen the album to compare its photos. It is possible that the album title is loose or that the collective showed something in the Veem that I could not find.

The 2017 album is the largest, with 113 photos by Max Kneefel, and its titles name guest academies including Bauhaus Universität, Burg Giebichenstein, Central Saint Martins and ECAL. Outside sources confirm the Veem for HOW&WOW that year, but I found none for the academies.
The 2018 album, titled Bauhaus Universität, has 13 photos by Kneefel, and each photo title names VEEM. HOW&WOW Studio was at the Veem that year.
The 2019 album has 22 photos, matching the Manifestations and HOW&WOW dates.
The 2022 album, VEEM - Manifestations, has 100 photos credited to about.today and Tommy Köhlbrugge.
The 2024 album has eight photos by Cleo Goossens, four titled with Veem and four with only Strijp-S.

The archive has no VEEM album for 2020, 2021, 2023 or 2025. The festival's own sites explain 2020 and 2021, since the exhibition was online in 2020 and at De Caai in 2021. For 2023 and 2025 they place Manifestations at the Veem, so those gaps look like gaps in the archive's list and not absences from the building, which fits the earlier note that the list I could read was incomplete.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: The register says 1942; the architects and the architecture center say 1943. I use 1942 and name the register.
2007 (competition) against 2009 (acquisition, per Strijp-S, Trudo and the renovation platform NRP). Not settled.
38, 39 or 40, from four descriptions of the same project; 39 has the most support.
Its title says Veem and two outside sources place that show elsewhere. Not settled.
Settled by the Canon and Omroep Brabant: Eindhoven sent experimental programs from 1948 to 1951, and the national start on October 2, 1951 came from Bussum.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have not seen the original construction drawings that the architects used, so I cannot describe the building's first layout beyond what the register and the journal say. I cannot say whether the guest academies of 2017 exhibited in it, or what the 2024 photos titled only Strijp-S show. I did not reopen the Flickr albums.

If you ride the lift to floor 8 during Dutch Design Week 2026, look at the columns and ask what they were built to carry. When a warehouse for finished goods becomes a food hall, a car park, a set of homes and a festival floor, which of those jobs would you say it was designed for?
